item.title: How to Live a Life You Would Never Have Chosen
item.description:
Chronic Illness

How to Live a Life You Would Never Have Chosen

A Personal Perspective: Is there a way forward for the chronically ill?

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic, debilitating illness is common and largely invisible.
  • Living this life entails reformating your days.
  • It also means finding acceptance amidst hope and meaning wihtin disability.
  • This is a personal journey but there are paths to choose from.
Ill every day.
Source: Karola/Pexels

Twenty years ago, I was diagnosed with a form of autoimmune arthritis. I’d had symptoms since college, but I had never been properly diagnosed. Two of my three brothers suffer from a form of the same disease. By the time of my diagnosis, it had seeped into every aspect of my life.

Up until then I was able to make accommodations through rest, early bedtimes, and appropriate exercise. However, in my early 40s, things heated up to the point that it became difficult to work. I have now been home and disabled for 13 years. On a good day, I may feel normal for a few hours in the afternoon. But if I overdo the most banal of activity, I will pay with more fatigue and joint pain later.

This is all to say that not feeling well and all the medical complications this entails are now the main subject of my life. As a psychiatrist who was in practice for 23 years, I am very familiar with people who are in a similar boat. Most of my patients did not feel well due to mental suffering (although some physical symptoms, such as fatigue, weakness, headache, and GI upset were common).

One thing all of us had in common was that the rest of the world had little awareness of our plight. In normal life, your body strikes a simple deal: give it ample rest and nutrition, and it allows you to go through your day and attend to what needs to be done without making a fuss. Other than meal and bedtime, it doesn’t bother you with demands for attention. When you are chronically ill, this is turned on its head. Your body demands attention like a fractious child. Due to its various aches and pains, it requires constant adjustments in your activity and mindset. Trying to feel better and dealing with how you feel is your full-time job.

Assuming, as is sadly the case, that many of these illnesses never get better, the question arises of how to live your life in the face of constant discomfort and a background of an increasing number of losses and limitations. For those of us in that situation, this is the real task of our days. The temptation and natural response is to try to feel better and imagine a better day just around the corner. But this makes you a hamster on a wheel.

What then is the path? Surely, we cannot give up some hope of improvement and attempts to stay healthy and, just perhaps, find a way forward. No, don’t give this up. Keep it on the back burner. But there is more work to be done.

The two central tasks of chronic illness are acceptance and a way to find meaning in a life you would never have chosen.

But don’t acceptance and hope contradict one another? How can we accept our losses, limitations and feeling poorly each day while we work and hope to improve our lot? The way to accomplish this is to remain aware that you are treading two paths. Yes, you must go to the doctor. Do your exercises and get a great deal of rest. You must avoid taxing situations and stay home a great deal of the time. Here, in fact, is where acceptance begins. It is exactly in living your life in ways that you would not choose where you seek to open yourself and accept your situation without a mental struggle. Letting go of this struggle does not mean letting go of hope for some change.

Acceptance includes a frank and often painful acknowledgment of where you are and what is lost to you. But in the long run, the pain of reliving your losses over and over is alleviated by acceptance. You must do your best to remain as healthy as possible while simultaneously acknowledging your limitations.

Part of this is a mourning process no different than the loss of a loved one. There is anger, bargaining, sadness, and hopefully acceptance. No more struggling with what might have been. This is harder for the chronically sick as the losses continue and some of these feelings will be revisited. That is part of the work.

When I first stopped working, I wondered how much more of myself could I lose and still feel like me. It turns out that I can lose a great deal and still be me. I have always understood myself as the sum of what I’ve accomplished in even one day. That obviously no longer works. You come to realize that despite your losses you remain yourself in the most fundamental of ways. How you treat people, what you value, and where you spend your limited attention continue to define you.

What I have found to be a more difficult question is finding meaning in your new existence. This is unfortunately an exercise that is not based on an equal distribution of luck in life. Those with more resources, more connections, and just plainly more opportunities have more chances of finding how to live a meaningful life. Here, as with anything else, you must play the cards you are dealt.

Meaning is based on values and will develop from what we find important. Interest and the involvement of other people are good places to start. But if you are stuck at home and cannot reliably get out to meetings, especially in the evening, how is this done? Unfortunately, there is no formula. Use of the Internet is a modern godsend to people like us. It makes possible connections to groups and causes that would otherwise be inaccessible. In addition, there are ways to learn new things, new skills, hobbies, etc.

There are times when this has felt to me like make-work. Usually, I have reverted to writing about psychiatry and illness, the two things I know and care about. But people vary a great deal in these personal matters. You do not need to start a charity, write a book, or learn a foreign language. Creativity, connecting to others, or just learning something new may bring new meaning to your days.

As I write this, though, it feels unsatisfactory. Recommending hobbies on YouTube does not truly feel like a way to find meaning, but rather more of a pastime. The very best suggestions I have given are not meaningful in and of themselves. Rather, they are pathways into your own deeper sense of importance and interest. This becomes a highly personal matter that only you can judge.

However personal and unique to you, it is an important part of your path through life with chronic illness. The journey is no longer through the outside world—as illness takes much of that away—but into yourself. The various pastimes are doorways into your internal life. This is where you now spend most of your time and where you must plant a flag to declare the continued importance of your very existence.

item.title: 5 Surprising Findings From the Science of Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

5 Surprising Findings From the Science of Happiness

A good life doesn’t always feel good.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • The shortest definition of well-being is to like one’s life.
  • A good life doesn’t always feel good.
  • Your values are more negotiable than you think.
  • We rank being morally good above feeling good. Our life satisfaction measures disagree.

The Norwegian town of Tromsø is home to the usual delights of a typical northern European city, and a few others one might expect of a place 300 kilometers north of the Arctic Circle. For example, from late November to mid-January, the sun never rises here. At the nearby UiT The Arctic University of Norway – the world’s northernmost university – psychologist Joar Vittersø has been studying the science of well-being for over 40 years. I asked him whether the winter’s veil of darkness affects him. Yes, he said, positively.

There’s much to like about polar night season – the snow, the beauty, the coziness of a slower pace, the contrast with what will follow. And for the negative elements, there’s adaptation. In fact, that people continue to be surprised by how readily they get used to things is among Vittersø’s own biggest surprises. Another of his insights is about the process of scientific progress. Human nature reveals itself gradually and knowledge is accrued “stone by stone.” Thankfully, “there’s an infinity to knowledge,” always something new to discover. This is good news for all of us – it keeps the well of engagement, interest and hope perpetually full.

Source: ekriksieart/pixabay

According to Vittersø, the shortest definition of well-being is to like one’s life. You have to like it hedonically, with all its joys and pleasures and satisfaction they bring, but also eudaimonically, for the opportunities it offers for growth and becoming a better person. And if the good life remains elusive, Vittersø thinks that might be partly due to our idealized fantasies of “true happiness” as something “extremely intense, rare and beautiful.” If that’s your idea, then you will be disappointed, he says, because emotions – whichever affective pole they lean towards – don’t last forever. Things are always in motion. Just like life under the northern skies of Tromsø, light and darkness take turns with their visits.

Here is Vittersø with five counterintuitive findings from the science of well-being.

1. A good life doesn’t always feel good.

This is surprising at first glance, but if you ask people how much sadness they would like in their perfect life, very few say zero – it’s somewhere between 1% and 5%. There are situations where happiness is simply not the appropriate response. We not only need negative feelings, but we also want them to some degree (but not too much). For example, we know that without one of the most intense negative feelings, namely pain, we wouldn’t survive. Pain is a signal that something is hurting us, and we need to deal with it. So, upon reflection, people realize that a good life is not the complete absence of negative feelings. We don’t only want happiness – we want a variety of emotions. Anything meaningful, like goals and relationships, requires effort and includes challenges.

2. Your values are more negotiable than you think.

Values are very complex. We have many of them, and we need them, but we can’t hold all of them in our attention at the same time. Thus, we organize them hierarchically, so that we can concentrate on particular values while doing our tasks. But if something else needs our attention – our child is crying or the fire alarm goes off – then the whole hierarchy reorders itself in a split second. I think that’s a very functional way for a mental system like the human brain to organize values: what matters most depends on the situation. It is important to remind ourselves about our values if we are tempted towards breaking them. Some values are moral: they oblige us to do things because they are right, not because they make us emotionally happy. I think the advice to “be true to your values” is about those we have reason to value – the values we agree about upon reflection. They are not necessarily identical to those that spontaneously come to mind.

3. Our lives are complex. Yet, we can spontaneously evaluate how satisfied we are with them.

When you ask people how satisfied they are with their lives, almost everyone can come up with an answer in a few seconds. Yet, we often struggle with simple everyday judgments, like which clothes to buy. But the notion of “life satisfaction” refers to an “all things considered” evaluation of your life as a whole, and surprisingly enough, we are able to make such judgments quickly and easily.

My theory is that this helps us survive. Judgements of good or bad come spontaneously, because we can’t stand there forever wondering whether a dangerous situation is good or bad. That capacity has evolved for a reason, and we are quite good at it. Life satisfaction responses resonate with many valuable things in life – but not all of them.

4. We rank being morally good above feeling good. Yet, our life satisfaction measures seem to disagree.

Source: eleatell/pixabay

Over the last years, I’ve asked participants in at least 15 different samples: If you had to choose between being a morally good person and being satisfied with your life, which is more important for you? In every study, 80 to 90 percent say being a morally good person. But when we ask about how morally good you would be in your perfect life versus how good you actually behave, most people have a gap. And you would predict that a big gap between your ideal and your current life would reduce life satisfaction. It hardly does. Hedonic gaps, however, affect us strongly.

I think one explanation is that life satisfaction comes from a spontaneous good-bad evaluation, while morality is determined by a right-wrong rationality. Including it requires us to pause and reflect on what we mean by “goodness.” That is enough to keep morality out of the spontaneous judgment, even if you personally think of it as an important value.

5. The good life is harder to measure than happiness surveys suggest.

The hedonic part of a good life is easy to measure but the eudaimonic elements are difficult. The essence of eudaimonia, to keep developing our human potential, doesn’t reveal itself easily in a survey. Yet, to understand the good life, we need both.

Many thanks to Joar Vittersø for his time and insights. Dr. Vittersø is Professor in Social Psychology at the Department of Psychology at UiT The Arctic University of Norway.

item.title: Are Our Shopping Decisions Really Our Own?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Are Our Shopping Decisions Really Our Own?

You’re under the influence, and often you don’t even know it.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Many psychological forces influence what we buy, and marketers know how to exploit them.
  • Promotional offers, emotions, our senses and even other people can influence shopping decisions.
  • We may never be uninfluenced, but understanding the science of why we buy can help us shop more thoughtfully.

Think about the last thing you bought. Perhaps it was something you needed, like groceries for dinner. Or something you wanted, like that impressive new smartphone, or something that's gone viral on social media that you didn't even know you needed but now suddenly want because everyone else in your feed has posted about it.

Whatever it was, you probably had a perfectly reasonable explanation for buying it. But was that explanation entirely yours, or did someone, or something else, influence your decision?

We're constantly being influenced by all kinds of psychological forces every day. Many of which big brands know exactly how to exploit, with one goal in mind: getting us to buy now and think later.

A discount can make something seem like a bargain, while a limited-time offer makes us rush to buy it before we've considered whether we need it.
Source: Max Fisher / Pexels

Why we buy what we buy

We like to believe we're rational shoppers, carefully weighing up what we need against what we can afford. Yet our brains are remarkably good at making irrational decisions, particularly when faced with more information and choices than we can comfortably process.

For example, consider the chaos that the Black Friday shopping event brings every year. We’re frantically browsing online and being bombarded with options when we see an exciting, time-limited promotional offer. Faced with a decision that suddenly feels urgent, we convince ourselves that we're saving money by taking advantage of the deal. Yet, in the rush to decide, we may fail to calculate just how much we’re saving or even consider if we're buying the thing we needed in the first place. We bought it just to avoid the pain of missing out or got swept up in the excitement of the deal.

Upgrading to a large coffee to go suddenly seems like excellent value when we realise it costs only a little more than the medium. Why wouldn't you pay a little more to get so much extra? But we've become so focused on the apparent bargain that we've failed to consider just how expensive the coffee was in the first place, or whether we can even physically drink that much. Chances are that the contents will go cold before we are able to finish it, wasting both coffee and money.

Our physical bodies can also be influenced to get us to buy more, like our emotions or senses. For example, we often look to what everyone else is buying when in a state of panic. During the COVID-19 pandemic, seeing others stockpile toilet paper could make us worry that there wouldn't be enough left for ourselves. No one stopped to question how toilet paper would keep us safe from the virus, but that wasn’t the point. Buying more than we needed influenced a sense of being in control at a time when society was locking down and our everyday freedoms were being restricted.

When it comes to influencing our senses, the smell of freshly baked bread or cookies drifting from the in-store bakeries in a supermarket can make us feel hungry, and a hungry shopper is a more impulsive one. Alternatively, slow-tempo music playing through the overhead speakers can subtly encourage us to move at a more leisurely pace around the store, increasing the time spent browsing all those products we didn't need but suddenly want now that we’ve seen them.

Even strangers on social media can influence what we buy
Source: Mart Production / Pexels

Then there are other people. Friends or even complete strangers on social media can influence us to buy the latest thing that's suddenly gone viral. Something as ordinary as a reusable tumbler can become a must-have product simply because everybody else seems to have one. We might not even need it, but owning one helps us feel part of the popular crowd.

We might believe we're choosing entirely for ourselves, but by the time we reach the checkout, an awful lot has already influenced what ends up in our shopping cart.

Who is really making the decisions?

None of this means that we're helpless consumers at the mercy of marketers when wandering around grocery stores or scrolling online during the dead of night.

We still have preferences, exercise judgment and ultimately decide whether or not to buy something. Nor is every influence necessarily harmful. A recommendation from a trusted friend might lead us to discover something perfect, or an eye-catching display might draw our attention to a genuinely better or cheaper product.

We can be influenced without being aware of it, but we can also recognise an influencing attempt and decide that we're perfectly happy to act on it. The more difficult question is whether we would have made the same decision if those influences hadn't been there at all.

Would we still have bought that large coffee if the medium hadn't been priced so closely to it? Would we have bought all that toilet paper if we didn’t see news reports of empty shelves and people bulk buying? Would the tumbler have seemed quite so appealing if we hadn't seen social media influencers telling us it was the next must-have thing?

The science of why we buy

These questions are at the heart of my new book, Influenced: The Science of Why We Buy.

There are so many strange and wonderful psychological forces that shape our purchasing decisions, from the mental shortcuts we rely on to make quick decisions to the influence of our emotions, our senses and the people we see online. All of this helps explain why we buy the things we do, like those purchases that seem perfectly sensible at the time but rather less so when we get home.

Perhaps we'll never be completely uninfluenced. After all, our decisions don't happen in isolation from the world around us. But understanding what shapes our choices give us an opportunity to question them and perhaps think a little more carefully before we reach for our wallets.

Ultimately, we may be the ones doing the shopping. That doesn't mean we're making every decision entirely on our own.

item.title: Beware of Rehab Recruitment Scams
item.description:
Addiction

Beware of Rehab Recruitment Scams

If you're considering addiction treatment, here are some red flags to watch for.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Treatment center scams, including impersonation and patient brokering, are widespread.
  • Call centers and even some treatment centers use keywords to impersonate other programs online.
  • These call centers, and some individuals working in or adjacent to recovery, receive kickbacks.
  • Body brokering, as it's called, is illegal, constituting a felony in some states.

Imagine you’ve been struggling with alcohol addiction. Every waking moment is spent either drinking or thinking about drinking. You don’t even want to drink anymore, but you just keep doing it. In a rare moment of lucidity, you decide it’s time to get help. This opportunity for help may come only once. Your life depends on getting genuine help right now.

But what if the person who answers the phone when you call is a salesperson, not a qualified admissions agent, and gets paid for every person they send to a specific program? What if the center offering the highest kickback this month provides a low quality of care or cuts you loose too soon? What if your family has spent their life savings to get you this care?

Situations like this are troublingly common. What’s behind them, and how can patients and their families avoid being scammed?

The Patient Experience

The following composite scenario lays out many of the practices involved in this kind of impersonation and the patient brokering that often follows.

A woman—we’ll call her Melissa—decides to seek help for opioid addiction. She googles a trusted treatment center in her town—we’ll call it Hometown Recovery—and dials the number that appears at the top of the page.

When an agent answers, Melissa breathes a sigh of relief. She believes she’s talking with someone at Hometown. The agent neither confirms nor denies Melissa’s assumption and asks what kind of insurance she has. If Melissa had Medicaid, that would likely be the end of the call. If she had private insurance, the agent would recommend a specific program “based on her insurance.”

But let’s say Melissa doesn’t have insurance at all. The agent offers to get insurance for her, for free. Melissa suspects something is off. She asks, “Is this Hometown Recovery?” The agent says, “We work with them. I can get you there,” and keeps asking questions. Melissa presses, and after she asks several times, the exasperated agent says, “Yes.”

Melissa accepts the offer for free insurance and is admitted to a program 600 miles away. She’s on a plane the next day and arrives just as withdrawal symptoms begin. She enters the center’s detox unit immediately.

In four days, she is thinking a little clearer. She wonders how she ended up here when she wanted to go to Hometown Recovery. She begins asking questions and ultimately says she wants to leave. Staff members respond that she needs to stay in detox for seven days because that’s what her insurance specified.

She agrees to stay, and at the end of seven days, she enters the center’s primary treatment program. She’s three weeks into residential care when the insurance company realizes her policy is fraudulent and cancels it. The profit-driven treatment center terminates her care. Melissa is far from home with no money, nowhere to go, and no way to get home.

Meanwhile, Hometown Recovery never heard from her. If Melissa has relatives back home who can help, she may be able to get there. But if—like so many people with her circumstances—she doesn’t have anyone, she is now homeless in a strange city after receiving partial treatment.

She took the brave step of asking for help, and she’s been robbed of an opportunity to heal. The call center hijacked her recovery, and this could prove fatal for Melissa.

Inside the Machine: Impersonation

Impersonation, in the business sense, involves one entity advertising or presenting as another. It’s often a way for unscrupulous businesses to capitalize on the good reputation of more established ones. In the treatment world, some independent or treatment-center-owned call centers buy ads using other centers’ exact names.

When Melissa googled her local treatment center, she saw an ad that read, “Hometown Recovery? Call Us Now!” But the call center she reached had purchased ads featuring “Hometown Recovery” as a keyword. This is an impersonation scam, and it’s illegal.

Perhaps worse than ad scams, some call centers impersonate free addiction helplines—someone trustworthy to talk to, confide in. And, like the search ad scammers, they recruit vulnerable people, either into the facility that operates the call center or the one paying the highest kickback. If you’re starting to feel as though these call centers are treating humans as a commodity, you’re not alone.

Inside the Machine: Patient Brokering

It’s truly appalling, but patient brokering (or body brokering) is when agencies or individuals receive kickbacks for funneling patients to specific treatment centers. So, instead of a person whose life is at stake being matched to the program that can best care for them, they’re turned over to the highest bidder.

Call centers are one patient brokering channel. But even police, people working in recovery, or those involved in meeting-based programs may receive kickbacks for recruitment. Likewise, some people who do street outreach—even very publicly on social media—are paid by treatment centers to bring in patients. Social media itself and websites disguised as general help are also common brokering channels.

Whether and how an influencer, agency, or trusted professional partners with those centers is scrutinized by a complex network of laws and regulations.

The Legal Landscape

What happened to Melissa likely violated several federal laws and regulations, as well as some state statutes, depending upon jurisdiction. And as you might expect, the most meticulous impersonators and brokers will operate in places where state laws are more favorable, or enforcement is low.

Federally, FTC truth-in-advertising laws apply to impersonation, and health care fraud statutes are commonly used to prosecute brokering. Both practices are getting more attention recently at the state level as well, and brokering is now a felony in a few states, including North Carolina, Florida, and Arizona.

With sentences ranging from probation to four years at the high end, it’s clear that brokering laws don’t have the teeth that they should, which is possibly one reason prosecutors seem to prefer fraud charges. Given the danger it can place vulnerable people in, including some documented cases of overdose death following brokered placements, consequences are insufficient to say the least. Some advocates and survivors make a compelling argument that brokering is indistinguishable from human trafficking.

Protecting Yourself and Your Loved Ones

With brokers potentially lurking everywhere, they may feel impossible to avoid. And the last thing we want to do is make patients or their families feel wary of every encounter—not trusting the whole industry could present a major barrier to receiving deeply needed care.

There are a few simple ways to spot scammers and brokers:

  • Get contact info only from the treatment center’s own website, never from other people or paid ads.
  • Don’t share any information over the phone before the agent tells you exactly what and where their program is.
  • If someone, even a healthcare or mental health professional, recommends a program, ask them if they get paid for referrals.

Report anything suspicious to the FTC and your state attorney general. Additionally, watch for the following red flags:

  • An agent answering the phone with a generic greeting like “Admissions,” or “Recovery helpline”
  • An offer to enroll you in insurance or pay your premiums
  • Free travel to out-of-state programs
  • Vagueness or inability to identify the treatment center by name
  • A brash, rude, or impatient demeanor on the phone

When you (or a loved one) reach out for help, the person receiving that call should always treat it as the only chance to save your life. The inhumanity of recovery impersonation scamming and patient brokering is hard to comprehend, but our hope is that knowing a bit about these practices will help you find the right treatment path.

item.title: Attention All Humans: AI Is Like a Spy
item.description:
Media

Attention All Humans: AI Is Like a Spy

Social media is designed to keep us scrolling, engaged, and enraged. Ads know it.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • AI technology constantly scans our online behavior.
  • Advertisers capitalize on our attention. Social media is designed to keep us engaged and enraged.
  • We are no longer consuming information but participating in a game designed to capture our attention.

Do you remember when it would take a minute or two for a website to fully load? The picture would reveal itself in incremental pixels until you could finally view it in its entirety. It was the era of banner ads and pop-ups, a rudimentary transference of billboard marketing to the World Wide Web.

Later, algorithms scanned, then shaped, our behavioral and consumption patterns. The length of time a user watched a video or stopped scrolling to “read more” became the metric for advertising effectiveness. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven technology measures how you behave online, like a little spy watching your every move without your noticing.

Welcome to the attention economy. “Pay attention!” the internet demands. “Or at least get paid for it,” advertising executives suggest. That is what influencer marketing is all about. The more clicks, the more views, the more money flows.

Reclaiming Attention

Joe Marchese and Jonathan Bing have penned a new book, Human Dot AI, that chronicles the rise of advertising from the era of Mad Men advertisers on Madison Avenue to today. Both authors have extensive experience in the industry themselves. Marchese is an entrepreneur and media executive, CEO of Human Ventures Holdings, co-founder of Casa Komos Brands Group, and chairman of Groundswell. He previously founded true[X] and led advertising revenue at Fox Networks Group. Bing is a marketing and communications executive who has held leadership roles at Netflix, 21st Century Fox, and Vice. He is also a journalist who has written for The New York Times, Los Angeles Times, and Wired. The authors wish to help readers reclaim their attention or, in their words, to “restore a sense of agency, choice, and control over the time and attention that algorithms are not designed to give you.”

Do you remember the ads “Have a Coke and a smile” or “I’d like to teach the world to sing in perfect harmony”? They lent viewers a sense of community and connection through catchy slogans and jingles that captured our collective imagination. Watching television, in a sense, was a shared experience. No fast-forwarding through commercials, no pre-recording to watch your favorite show at a later time. The Super Bowl remains an exception as one of the most popular live televised sports events of the year in which the legendary commercials running at roughly $10 million per 30-second slot are often as memorable as the game itself. According to Nielsen, a global leader in measuring audience behavior, however, nearly half of all TV viewers have switched to streaming services such as Netflix and YouTube. In a recent video call, Marchese admitted that consuming social media today "is like watching television," but not in the same way we used to in the pre-Internet era. Today, asynchronous viewing has made watching programs a much more isolating experience.

Source: The Nielsen Company (US)/used with permission.

With 5.8 billion mobile phone users worldwide, 70 percent of the planet’s population has a robust digital communications-based lifestyle. Marchese and Bing aim to offer a way back to human connection despite our AI-saturated lives. Around the time that Facebook’s News Feed feature was launched (yes, there was a time when you actually had to actively look for people by clicking on various profiles), it stopped being a place to connect and became more a place to advertise, albeit subtly. Advertising became adjacent to social activity itself, deeply embedded in the content without our realizing it. Consumer engagement became the name of the game. No more annoying pop-up ads. Enter the gamification of social media consumption. We are no longer simply consuming information (and patiently waiting for pictures to load); we are now participating in a game designed to capture and retain our attention—all day long. As a result, two problems have emerged: the lack of editorial supervision and the machines’ lack of understanding humans. Content is no longer about bringing people together but, rather, about keeping people engaged and enraged.

Algorithms Cannot Replace Human Connection

“[N]o algorithm can replace what happens when people come together around something real—a shared experience, story, or glass” (Marchese & Bing, 2026). An automated, algorithm-driven life flattens intimacy, commercializes our need for connection, and monetizes our very human desire to love and be loved. How we spend our time and attention truly matters. These resources are finite, but an algorithm doesn’t care why a user is engaged with the content. It is designed to feed us more of the same.

Digital hygiene is key to maintaining a sense of equilibrium in our tech-driven lives. Attention-grabbing is as old as the advertising industry itself. From the town crier to our social media apps, brands yearn for our attention. But in the end, we, as humans, get to decide if we give it or not.

item.title: You’re Making Big Decisions for a Person You’ve Never Met
item.description:
Identity

You’re Making Big Decisions for a Person You’ve Never Met

You can see how much you’ve changed. You can’t see how much you still will.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • At every age, people report significant past change but predict far less change ahead.
  • We explain our future selves the way we explain strangers: from the outside.
  • Children show the same blind spot about themselves, but not about other people.
  • Interventions that build connection to your future self are less proven than they sound.
Source: Look Studio / Unsplash

The life I had at 22, along with the one I pictured ahead of me, no longer exists.

I was living in New York City, auditioning weekly for commercial dance roles and cruise-line troupes while pursuing my degree in creative writing. I’d spent years learning how to pick up choreography in 15 minutes and write a poem that holds a feeling it never names. If you had told that person she would end up doing neuropsychological evaluations in a Boston hospital, she would not have believed you, because she could not have pictured it.

She knew who she was at that time, but she was simultaneously wrong about what her future would look like.

Psychologists have a name for this failure of vision: the end-of-history illusion. It's the tendency to recognize how much you have changed while predicting that the changing is now largely over. In six studies with more than 19,000 people aged 18 to 68, participants at every age reported substantial change over the previous decade and yet forecast far less for the decade ahead. A 30-year-old looks back at 20 and sees a different person. She looks forward to 40 and sees her present self, slightly adjusted.

The pattern held for personality traits, core values, and everyday preferences. It held for the 18-year-olds and for the 68-year-olds. Everyone, apparently, believes they have just now arrived at the finished version.

The lease is 30 years long, and you are signing it on behalf of someone you have never met. That is the practical problem, as the decisions that bind hardest tend to cluster in your late twenties and thirties: the mortgage, the specialty, the city, the degree, the name, the person. You make them with full information about your current preferences and almost no imagination for your future ones.

Your future self is filed under other people

The more unsettling finding is who we think we are predicting for.

Emily Pronin and Lee Ross found that when people describe their future selves, they reach for the same explanatory style they use for strangers. We explain our current behavior by pointing to circumstances: the week was brutal, the request was unreasonable. We explain other people’s behavior by pointing to their character. And we explain our future selves’ behavior the way we explain others: from the outside.

A 2024 study found the end-of-history pattern in children as young as four, across two experiments with 256 participants, including a design in which the same child was asked about both past and future. A third experiment asked children about other people. In that study, the illusion disappeared. Children can imagine that someone else will change, but can’t see their own change coming.

What we learned from this study is that the future version of you gets handled by the part of your mind that imagines people you have not met.

The temptation to fix it

There is a whole literature on closing the gap, built around what researchers call future self-continuity, or how connected you feel to the person you will become. The interventions are inventive: writing a letter to yourself 20 years out, viewing an age-progressed photograph. More recently, a team at MIT built a system that lets you hold a conversation with an AI-generated version of yourself at 60; in a preregistered study of 344 young adults, a single session lowered reported anxiety and raised a sense of connection to the future self.

However, in late 2025, a team went looking for studies that had tested these techniques. They screened more than 1,200 papers and found 14. Fewer than half of those bothered to check whether the exercise had actually changed how connected participants felt to their future selves, which was the whole premise. And nearly all the participants were college students in their twenties. Not one study asked whether this works differently at 40.

In other words, the technique that makes you feel closer to your future self has not been shown to make you better at predicting it.

What to do instead

I don’t think you need to successfully forecast the person you will be in 2036, and the research gives no reason to think you could.

The goal is to have humility about the forecast you are making. When you make a decision that binds, beyond choosing between options, you’re making a prediction that the person living with the consequences will want what you want today. The research has shown that prediction is almost certainly too confident.

Decisions differ in what they cost if you change. A lease and a mortgage both bind you, but one releases you in a year. A degree and a license both take years, but only one of them travels. That difference is a property of the decision rather than of the person making it.

So extend some grace backward. The decisions you now find baffling were made by someone operating with the same blind spot you have right now, and they were doing their best with a self they could not see past.

My creative-writing major self was not wrong. She just could not have known that learning to read a line for what it does not say would turn out to be useful in a room where someone is describing their memory loss and leaving out the part that frightens them.

item.title: When Grief Changes a Family, Does Distance Mean Love Is Lost?
item.description:
Grief

When Grief Changes a Family, Does Distance Mean Love Is Lost?

Sibling relationships, grief, and the importance of giving family room to change.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Family members respond to loss in different ways, sometimes creating tension or distance in relationships.
  • Healthy families allow room for individuality and changing needs without losing relationship significance.
  • Meaningful support comes from being present, listening, and allowing loved ones to grieve in their own way.

When a family member dies, we may imagine the surviving family members leaning on one another, sharing memories, and finding comfort in their common loss. This doesn’t always happen, as grief doesn't always bring families closer. In some cases, it creates more distance between the people who might understand our loss best.

An empty bench in a park
Source: A. Karnholz / Adobe Stock

In Hallmark's "A Season of Promises," sisters Heidi and Sophie have grown apart following their mother's death four years ago. We see their obvious differences while we watch a home video from 30 years ago. Viewers may expect the sisters to have their issues, but we soon learn that they no longer interact after the death of their mother. They reach out to one another only after their father, Ed, experiences a health scare. After realizing how alone he is, they decide to help him find love again while also encouraging him to seek out grief support.

While the movie follows their matchmaking efforts, its more interesting story is about what happens to family relationships after a significant loss. It portrays three family members who experienced the same loss and who are grieving in three very different ways.

When One Loss Changes Every Relationship

The death of a family member doesn't simply remove one person from a family. Instead, it changes the relationships among everyone who remains. Family systems theory suggests that families are interconnected systems. When something happens to one member, the effects ripple throughout the family. The loss of a parent, for example, may change how siblings interact, how responsibilities are distributed, and how family members understand their new roles. Family members grieve not only the person who moved on but also the role they no longer occupy.

The Double ABC-X model of family stress can also help explain why some families struggle following a loss. Families must manage not only the original stressful event but also the additional demands that accumulate afterward. Their ability to adapt depends partly on available resources and how family members interpret their circumstances. Sometimes, the difficulty isn't that family members don't care about one another. It's that they don't know how to support one another when their needs are different.

Sibling Relationships: Our Longest Relationships

Heidi (D’Orsay) and Sophie (Liebert)
Source: Hallmark Media

For many people, sibling relationships are the longest-lasting relationships in their lives. Siblings often know us before our friendships, romantic partnerships, and professional identities develop. They share family histories, childhood experiences, and memories that no one else can fully replicate, but the length of a relationship does not mean its closeness will remain constant.

Sibling relationships often move through periods of connection and disengagement. Geographic distance, different life circumstances, competing responsibilities, and unresolved disagreements can all influence how frequently siblings interact. Heidi and Sophie are examples. Although their relationship has become strained, the distance isn’t permanent, as their concern for their father brings them together again. Sophie’s love interest made a particularly meaningful observation, after listening to her discuss her complicated sibling relationship: "Families are messy. It doesn't mean you stop loving each other."

I appreciated Hallmark including this interaction because so many of us feel like having messy families signals trouble, but it’s a reality of having complex and interdependent relationships that can be impacted by stressors. Sophie's and Heidi’s relationship captures the reality of relationships. They also demonstrate the notion that love and closeness are not necessarily the same thing. We can love family members deeply while needing distance from them. We can disagree about the past without erasing the relationships that shaped us. Disengagement is not always a sign that a relationship has failed. Sometimes it reflects a period when family members need space to manage their own lives, emotions, or identities.

Closeness Needs Flexibility

The Circumplex Model of Marital and Family Systems identifies two important dimensions of family functioning: cohesion and flexibility. Cohesion describes the emotional bonds among family members. Flexibility refers to a family's ability to adjust its roles, relationships, and expectations when circumstances change.

Healthy family relationships generally require a balance of both. Too little cohesion (i.e., disengagement) may leave family members feeling disconnected, while too much cohesion (e.g., enmeshment) may make it difficult for individuals to develop independence or establish boundaries.

Similarly, families that struggle to adapt may find themselves expecting relationships to remain exactly as they were, even after significant life changes. For Heidi and Sophie, rebuilding their relationship doesn't necessarily mean returning to the closeness they experienced before their mother's death. Instead, it may require recognizing that they have changed and allowing their relationship to change with them.

Connection leaves room for individuality. Family members do not have to experience grief identically, make the same decisions, or maintain constant contact to remain important to one another.

Sometimes Love Means Sitting With Grief

Perhaps one of the movie's most insightful moments occurs when one of the daughters confides in a new love interest that she wants to fix her father's grief. He gently suggests that perhaps her father doesn't need someone to fix his grief and that maybe he needs someone willing to sit in it with him. This distinction is important.

When someone we love is hurting, our instinct is often to make the pain disappear. We offer solutions, encourage new activities, or try to help them move forward. These efforts usually come from a place of love, but they may also reflect our own discomfort with watching someone suffer. Grief, however, is not a problem that another person can solve.

Social support can help people cope with loss, but support doesn't always require action. Sometimes it means listening without offering advice, acknowledging difficult emotions, or simply being present. The sisters' efforts to find their father a romantic partner reflect their desire to see him happy again, but his grief cannot necessarily be resolved by introducing someone new into his life. A new relationship may bring joy, but it doesn't erase the significance of the relationship that was lost.

Making Room for a Different Relationship

Hallmark movies typically offer satisfying resolutions, and A Season of Promises is no exception. The movie raises a question that extends beyond its Christmas setting: What does it mean to remain a family when our relationships no longer look the way they did? Families experience periods of closeness, conflict, loss, and disengagement. Not every disagreement can be resolved immediately, and not every relationship will return to its previous form.

Maintaining family relationships can mean accepting that people grieve differently, need different amounts of connection, or require time apart. What matters is whether family members can make room for one another's needs while being honest about their own. Perhaps the lesson of A Season of Promises isn't that families must always come back together. Instead, it’s that relationships can change without losing their significance.

Hallmark vs. Psychology

Hallmark says: A loved one's health scare can be the catalyst to bring a family back together, along with the help of Christmas magic.

Psychology says: Family relationships don't have to remain consistently close to be meaningful. Healthy families make room for different experiences of grief, changing relationships, and the understanding that supporting someone doesn't always mean fixing their pain.

The verdict: Hallmark captures the complexity of grief and how differently it can be experienced within the same family. The movie portrays a family struggling with loss, the ways grief can strain relationships, and the challenges of grieving both individually and together. Ultimately, the family comes to recognize that moving forward doesn't mean returning to how things were before their loss. Instead, they learn to embrace a new normal, one that makes room for grief, changing relationships, and continued love.

item.title: Does the Space Where We Deliver Therapy Matter?
item.description:
Therapy

Does the Space Where We Deliver Therapy Matter?

The space where therapy happens affects therapeutic relationships and wellbeing.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • The physical environment in which therapy happens can affect treatment effectiveness and personal well-being.
  • Therapists' duty of care extends to those who may inadvertently overhear client conversations.
  • Therapy rooms must accommodate what treatment is delivered and how, not determine it.
  • Providing appropriate facilities is an ethical and professional responsibility.

Picture yourself trying to discuss your deepest anxieties with your therapist while a conversation about last night’s TV can be heard outside the door. How about attempting a therapeutic exercise in a room barely large enough for two chairs?

A number of therapists have raised concerns to me about the spaces in which they are expected to work.

Some report being expected to conduct telephone or online sessions in settings where conversations could be overheard by colleagues or others nearby. Others describe working in noisy buildings, sharing spaces with services that have very different needs, or using communal waiting areas, which can unsettle clients and disrupt sessions.

Changes to room layout, size, availability and accessibility have also raised concerns. These situations can arise when therapy services face growing demand for appointments and staff must share limited facilities for face-to-face, telephone and online sessions.

The space in which therapy takes place really does matter.

Confidentiality is more than closing the door

Protecting a client’s confidentiality is a foundational principle of psychological therapy.

The ethical principles of acting in the client’s best interests, doing good, avoiding harm and acting fairly may all be compromised if private conversations can be overheard.

Telephone appointments carried out in call-center style settings can increase the good done for a larger number of people by widening access to psychological therapies, particularly in high-volume, low-intensity services—but this must not come at the expense of confidentiality.

Clients are assured that their conversations will remain private but hearing background noises during a call could undermine that assurance. Even if a client is unaware that others are within earshot, therapists still have a duty to protect their confidentiality. If conversations can be overheard, this professional responsibility could be compromised.

There is also the potential for impact on those who inadvertently overhear confidential, sensitive, or distressing information.

In a face-to-face session, hearing footsteps passing along the corridor outside may not be particularly disruptive. But loud noises, conversations outside the door, or interruptions can break the focus of both the therapist and client, affect their relationship, and interfere with the session’s progress.

Is the room a barrier to progress?

Room size and accessibility are not just administrative matters. They can also raise ethical concerns.

A cramped consulting room may be inaccessible or uncomfortable for a client or therapist who needs additional space, uses mobility aids, or requires another person to be with them in the room.

Is there enough room for an interpreter, family member, advocate, or even clinical supervisor for the duration of the session if necessary?

The nature of the issues being addressed may influence how comfortable the client may feel sitting close to someone else.

For those who have experienced a trauma or have cultural expectations about maintaining a respectful distance, being forced to sit very close to someone else, even if that person is their therapist, will be hard to accommodate in a small room and may affect their ability to fully engage in the session.

Even seemingly small details can have an impact. For example, are there windows and natural light? Is the space well-ventilated and kept at a comfortable temperature? An enclosed space may be uncomfortable for someone experiencing high levels of anxiety, while poor ventilation could increase the risk of transmitting infection. Small or unsuitable rooms could have a disproportionate and potentially discriminatory effect on clients who are traumatised, have disabilities, are neurodivergent or need additional support.

They may also create barriers for therapists with protected characteristics.

Does the room support the therapy?

Therapy is not always just two people sitting opposite each other and talking. Depending on the treatment, therapist and client may need to move around, manoeuvre a wheelchair, take pacing breaks, carry out behavioural experiments or exposure exercises, or use techniques such as the empty chair exercise. The space should accommodate the required activities rather than dictate them.

Therapists may also need recording equipment or access to online or written materials.

Furniture matters too: A desk for being able to take notes, different types of seating, a coffee table, or a whiteboard may all play a part in delivering effective therapy.

Although perhaps less common than cramped rooms, a very large space could also present challenges. Unless the extra space is needed for the work being carried out, it may make it harder to create a comfortable, supportive ambiance in a clinical session.

Then there is room availability. Limited access to suitable rooms, or competition to book them at key times, can affect appointment availability and, therefore, clients’ access to therapy and the effective delivery of treatment. The knock-on effect of this is to add to pressures on practitioners and affect their wellbeing.

Always thinking about professional standards

The space in which therapy is delivered matters, as it can affect the quality and safety of care, equity, client choice, and practitioner well-being.

To meet professional standards of conduct, performance and ethics, therapy services have a responsibility to provide accommodation that supports safe, effective, equitable and sustainable psychological therapies, as well as meeting legal obligations.

Practitioners and service leaders can draw on organisational and professional standards, best practice guidelines and NHS guidance on suitable accommodation when considering how to address or avoid any concerns.

Ensuring workplaces provide suitable spaces can support practitioners’ wellbeing and fitness to practice, reduce the risk of burnout and enhance the service provided to clients.

Questions for reflection

  • If you were experiencing these challenges, what steps would you take next?
  • How can the ethical decision-making steps outlined help with deciding what to do?
  • As a peer or trusted colleague, how would you respond if someone raised concerns about their clinical working environment?
  • Could clinical supervision offer a safe opportunity to reflect on the steps needed to ensure that therapy spaces support good standards of care and practitioner wellbeing?
  • Finally, having addressed the immediate concerns, what could be learned to improve the environment for clients and practitioners in the future?
Helen Macdonald
Source: BABCP

Helen Macdonald is a BABCP-accredited Cognitive Behavioural Psychotherapist Supervisor and Trainer, a consultant EMDR Therapist, and Senior Clinical Advisor to the BABCP. As a prominent voice within the organisation, she frequently hosts the “Members Matters” podcast.

item.title: 5 Ways to Handle Problems That Keep Coming Back
item.description:
Self-Help

5 Ways to Handle Problems That Keep Coming Back

Every struggle can reveal what matters most and offer a path toward growth.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Recurring struggles can reveal personal values and help clarify what deserves your attention.
  • Some unwanted behaviors persist because they help us avoid discomfort or meet an underlying need.
  • Shifting attention beyond what's wrong can create a more balanced and compassionate perspective.
  • Accepting what cannot be changed can free up energy for meaningful action and personal growth.

When I planted my fall garden here in Santa Barbara, I was most excited about the sunflowers. I had finally solved the problem of our ground squirrels. My bedroom window looks out over the garden, and now the sunflowers are a good five feet tall, with buds forming. When I wake up in the morning, they are the first thing I look for.

Except, smack in the middle of my view is some construction workers’ porta-potty.

Many mornings I look out there, hoping to see a sunflower, and instead I see an electrician exiting, pulling up his fly.

Such is our experience in life. Just as soon as we solve one problem, another one is blocking our way, interrupting our happiness.

Before I go on, consider this:

  • What are the sunflowers in your life right now?
  • What is the porta-potty?

Problems are like ground squirrels, and the construction workers, they keep coming back and you don’t get to decide when. So, what should we do when they do? Here are five things to consider, based on my Wise Effort method, and thousands of hours of listening to people’s problems (plus thousands of hours complaining about mine).

1. Beneath every problem is a value.

It wouldn’t be a problem if it didn’t matter to you in some deeper way. Try ranting about your problem for one minute (yes, set at timer) and then ask yourself: What does this reveal that I care about?

Now you have something more useful than a complaint. You have a direction.

2. Your problem is working for you in some way.

Strange loops, vicious cycles, negative reinforcement, experiential avoidance, secondary gain—whatever psychological term you want to use, some problems stick around because they are solving other problems. How is your problem working for you? That construction worker is fixing my house, afte rall—and that fight you pick with your husband on Sunday night? It might just be serving you in some roundabout way too.

What is your struggle helping you avoid or what are you getting out of it?

Once you understand what the problem is doing for you, you have more freedom to choose another way.

3. You may need to adjust your focus.

Sometimes your problems keep coming back, because you are a problem search engine: You are only looking for things that are going wrong. Attention is like a spotlight. You can narrow it down to one tiny thing, or you can widen the lens and let it illuminate the whole picture. In Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, we call these processes flexible perspective-taking and flexible attention. When you can move your focus around—out and in, right and left, narrow and wide—how you see your problem will likely shift. Often it shifts toward something more balanced or compassionate.

4. Our minds love to create and solve problems.

The brain seeks stimulation, control, and something to do. And if there isn’t a problem available, it may create one. Life hands us problems, sure. But is it really a problem that the plane is late? Haven’t you been wanting, more than anything, a little time to do nothing? Is it really a problem that your teen is aloof? Aren’t you going to miss them when they are gone? Sometimes what is wrong is simply that your mind is looking for something wrong.

5. Some problems can be solved. Some cannot.

The word “acceptance” is in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for a reason. Often the pathway to commitment and change is acceptance. Acceptance means allowing what is already here to be part of your experience so you can stop spending all your energy arguing with reality. It means making room for the full experience: irritation and gratitude, beauty and inconvenience, sunflowers and porta-pottys.

And sometimes, when you accept, move toward, and allow the very thing you fear or hate, you end up back at the beginning.

Beneath every problem is a value. As Pema Chödrön writes, “things come together and they fall apart.” Then they come together again. Then they fall apart again:

  • Beneath every problem is a value
  • Your problem is working for you in some way
  • You may need to adjust your focus
  • Some problems cannot be solved

Takeaway practice

This week, choose one problem that has been taking up a lot of your energy

Then ask:

What value is underneath this problem?

How is this problem working for me?

Can I see it differently?

What story am I adding?

Can I make room for it?

Your task is to become more skillful with the problems you have, so they can become gateways to your values and you can keep tending your little garden patch with care.

item.title: The Ancient Secret to Calm and Courage
item.description:
Fear

The Ancient Secret to Calm and Courage

What Socrates the soldier understood about fear.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Socrates was not just a philosopher, but a seasoned soldier who distinguished himself in battle.
  • For Socrates, courage was not fearlessness, but knowing what is truly worth fearing.
  • Socrates remained faithful to his convictions even when doing so cost him his life.
Ancient Greek hoplite helmet. Socrates fought in at least three military campaigns and was renowned for his courage and composure.
Source: Neel Burton. AI-generated.

In 424 BCE, the Athenian army suffered a crushing defeat at Delium. As the soldiers fled the battlefield, one man stood out for his extraordinary composure. He was neither a famous general nor a celebrated warrior, but a middle-aged philosopher.

According to the officer Alcibiades, who witnessed the retreat from horseback, Socrates walked away with such calm and confidence that the enemy soldiers left him alone, preferring to pursue those who were fleeing in panic.

It was not the first time Socrates had distinguished himself in battle. Nor would it be the last.

Socrates at War

We tend to picture Socrates as an old man in the marketplace, questioning his fellow Athenians about courage, justice, and the good life. But he did not merely talk about courage; he demonstrated it.

Like many Athenian citizens, Socrates trained as a hoplite, a heavily armed foot soldier who fought in the close formation known as the phalanx. He fought in at least three campaigns: Potidaea, Delium, and Amphipolis.

The earliest of these, the siege of Potidaea, began in 432 BCE, when Socrates was about 38 years old. The siege was long and arduous, with the soldiers exposed to hunger, cold, and disease.

In Plato’s Symposium, Alcibiades recalls that Socrates endured these hardships much better than anyone else in the army. During a severe frost, he marched barefoot over the ice, apparently indifferent to the cold. His comrades looked daggers at him, thinking that he was showing them up.

Yet, Socrates was no joyless ascetic. Alcibiades adds that no one enjoyed a festival more than he did. If called upon, he could drink everyone under the table—although no one had ever seen him drunk.

At Potidaea, Socrates also saved Alcibiades’ life. But when the generals awarded the prize for valour to the high-born Alcibiades, Socrates insisted that Alcibiades should keep it.

Here was a man who could endure almost anything, enjoy almost anything, and yet remain master of himself. No wonder Alcibiades was in love with him. To everyone's shock, Alcibiades even shared a tent with him.

What Is Courage?

It is hardly surprising that a man with so much experience of war should have thought deeply about courage.

In Plato’s Laches, Socrates discusses the nature of courage with two distinguished generals, Laches and Nicias.

At first, courage might seem easy enough to define. Surely, it consists in standing one’s ground against the enemy, or in remaining fearless in the face of danger?

But Socrates is not so sure. After all, a man might remain fearless out of foolishness or recklessness. He might be fearless simply because he does not understand the danger he is in. Would we call such a man courageous?

After a time, Nicias proposes that courage is a kind of knowledge: knowledge of what is truly to be feared and hoped for.

Socrates finds this definition more promising, but points out that such knowledge cannot be confined to the future. To know what is truly to be feared and hoped for, we must also know what is truly good and bad. Therefore, courage, if it is to be called courage, is born out of knowledge in general.

Socrates notices that, in trying to define courage, they have stumbled upon two larger ideas. First, the virtues are closely related. To be truly courageous, we must also be wise, just, and self-controlled. This is known as the unity of the virtues. Courage is not simply the ability to face danger, but the wisdom to know whether the danger ought to be faced. Second, deep down, all the classical virtues—courage, justice, piety, temperance—amount to knowledge and wisdom.

But is knowledge alone enough? Might it not be possible to understand what is right and true and still lack the courage to act upon it? For Socrates, if we truly know what is right and true, we cannot fail to act upon this knowledge. But in Plato’s Republic, courage takes on a further dimension: the preservation of our convictions about what is and is not to be feared, despite our desires, fears, and baser instincts. This, if you like, is a kind of meta-courage: the courage to remain faithful to one’s understanding of what matters.

As I discuss in my book, The Gang of Three, calm and courage begin with knowing what is truly worth fearing and meeting it with wisdom rather than fear. The less we depend on comfort, approval, and other things we might lose, the less we have to fear, and the more freely and courageously we can live.

The Courage to Die

In 399 BCE, Socrates was put on trial for impiety and corrupting the youth. Facing the possibility of execution, he refused to abandon philosophy or say what was needed to save his life.

Instead, he reminded the jury that, just as he had not deserted his post at Potidaea or Delium for fear of death, so he would not now desert his lifelong convictions.

For Socrates, to fear death was to pretend to know what we do not know. Death might be an evil, but it might equally be a blessing. What we do know is that injustice is an evil, and that it is better to suffer an injustice than to commit it.

When Socrates was condemned to death, he had the means to escape, but chose instead to drink of the poisoned cup.

With the same extraordinary composure, the man who had faced death for Athens now faced death at the hands of Athens. He had not merely talked about courage, or even demonstrated it on the battlefield. He had carried it through to the very end.

It’s quite a thought that, had Socrates fallen in battle, or, at the end, played the part of a coward, we today would be living in different minds, in a different world.

You may also enjoy my companion piece, Why Socrates Chose to Die.

item.title: My Health Anxiety Frustrates My Doctor; Now What?
item.description:
Anxiety

My Health Anxiety Frustrates My Doctor; Now What?

How we respond to physician invalidation is a matter of autonomy.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that medical invalidation and poor bedside manner are problematic for anxious patients.
  • Asymmetric patient-provider relationships can worsen an anxious patient's medical fears.
  • Self-determination and autonomy are important for patients to ensure an empathetic clinical relationship.

When the cardiologist frustratedly told me, “Look, I can’t tell you what every little thing you feel in your chest is,” I immediately felt invalidated, shamed, and guilty for having wasted his time. But I had been feeling discomfort in my chest for a while, and my primary care physician had referred me to a cardiologist as a precautionary measure. I was only following doctor’s orders. While the wisdom of hindsight tells me that I was experiencing anxiety, not a cardiac problem, I did not know it at the time, and I was relying on the cardiologist to give me some peace of mind, not to make me feel silly.

A Common Experience

Many individuals who experience health anxiety have been in similar situations where a medical professional’s reaction has left them feeling worse rather than better at a medical appointment. There is a substantial body of research to support the idea that provider invalidation, dismissiveness, and lack of empathy are not only not uncommon but also make an already stressful situation for a health-anxious person even worse. A 2022 study concluded that “patients felt dismissed when they perceived that providers were rude or did not take action, provided poor information, did not believe patients, rushed the visit, or were uninformed" (Hildenbrand et al., 2022). A systematic review of 57 qualitative studies on the topic concluded that “due to the asymmetric physician-patient relationship, physicians should strive to treat patients with dignity and respect in order to alleviate the harmful effects of negative experiences” (Rocque & Leanza, 2015). Provider invalidation, such as that displayed by my cardiologist, is a serious problem for individuals who are already anxious about their health status.

It’s Not About Them

So, what can a patient do if they find themselves in a clinical relationship with an invalidating provider? First, a recognition of a patient’s autonomy is necessary; patients must view the relationship from a place of equal footing and reframe the aforementioned “asymmetric physician-patient relationship.” Two human beings are in a medical office, both of whom deserve common courtesy. I like to remember that my medical appointments are about me, not the doctor. With this mindset, I can be less concerned about “annoying” or “bothering” my provider. My provider is there to provide services to me, and I have the freedom to ask what I need to ask, to express concern, or to seek reassurance. The doctor, in turn, has an obligation to treat my concerns respectfully and seriously, and to utilize a bedside manner that is appropriate and ethical.

It’s OK to Make a Change

We sometimes feel that once we have established a clinical relationship with a provider, we should maintain it even if we are unhappy with the service. Health-anxious people can feel a sense of obligation to their provider and a hesitation to question them or to seek out other opinions. If, however, you feel that your provider is not being appropriately attentive to your concerns or is behaving in an invalidating or dismissive manner, you have the freedom to change providers or seek a second opinion. Often, individuals feel that they are doing something “wrong” or “betraying” their doctor if they make a change, but the reality is that those who provide our services are not always the best match for us. And, particularly in medical matters, we have the autonomy and freedom to change course or go a different route to find a medical relationship that better aligns with our needs.

Your Medical Care Is Yours

When it comes to your health, your medical care belongs to you. If, for instance, you wanted all your medical records, you are allowed to request them, and they must be provided by your provider—they belong to you by law. This sense of full autonomy is often forgotten by anxious patients, but reframing the experience of being a patient through a lens of autonomy and agency can be helpful in restoring a sense of self-governance. I am proud to say that my response to that cardiologist’s behavior was to seek a different one, and it was my self-determination that allowed me to recognize that I had no obligation to stay with an invalidating doctor and that it was my decision to go somewhere I would be treated more empathetically. Do not forget that, as a patient, you possess full autonomy.

What You Deserve

Anxiety can rob us of our voice, make us feel that we should “hold it together,” and keep us from advocating for ourselves. But just because you have health anxiety does not mean you need to have a doctor who makes you feel worse. Our physical health is precious, and we all deserve to feel that it is being treated in a respectful and ethical way. Please remember that you deserve empathic care—even if you are an anxious patient. Many researchers agree that there is a “need for better support in developing empathic skills” among physicians (Gössi et al., 2025). In the meantime, you—the patient—can ensure that your medical care is reassuring, not triggering or invalidating.
