item.title: I'm a Therapist, and I Tested AI as My Therapist
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

I'm a Therapist, and I Tested AI as My Therapist

I went into the experiment with an open mind. Here's what happened.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • AI may validate your feelings without considering your best interests.
  • Feeling understood by AI doesn't mean you're receiving sound advice.
  • When it comes to communication skills, using AI effectively might require questioning and refining its output.
Source: Image generated by ChatGPT

I ran my own informal experiment using AI as my "therapist." I get it if you’re thinking, “Oh, she's a therapist—of course she's going to tell me AI therapy is bad.” Honestly, I was open to the experience, and I was surprised by the excellence of a few of the responses.

Here’s some background: I first used the AI chatbot as my emotional trashcan. Without providing identifying information, I vented my anger enough to settle my system so I could move to the next step: giving the AI a prompt addressing a real and personal communication issue I was working through.

Communication and boundary-setting are common topics in therapy. I shared some of the history of the interpersonal dynamics between this person and me, along with my current boundary-setting and communication goals, which included not setting off an emotional firestorm or inviting more back-and-forth. I then asked it what I could say.

The chatbot first provided emotional validation, which seemed excessive to me: “This sounds so painful!” followed by paragraphs of sycophancy, which is not surprising given the research on how AI tends to communicate. It took it a while to get to my actual task.

Importantly, the advice regarding what to say could have blown up the relationship I was seeking advice about. Granted, AI was textbook fabulous at validating my feelings. However, it aligned way too much with my emotions and not with my actual aims, a concern raised in some research on AI and relationships. For instance, it encouraged me to 1) say you-statements that could have easily been read as accusatory or provocative, and 2) provide too many details that would likely lead the person to focus on debating those details over receiving the boundary. Ummmm, no.

Fortunately, due to my training in communication and clinical skills, I could stop, reflect, and correct.

I found that the AI suggestions improved as I narrowed the prompts and got more and more specific. Examples included requests such as “The section starting with X concerns me. How can I say it in a gentler way, using I-statements?” “Please explore how a person who tends to respond defensively might respond to this statement,” and “Apply this communication to a person with narcissistic traits." I added the narcissistic traits comment to see if AI would use it as a pop-culture reference, a description, a diagnosis, or something else.

It argued against my “narcissistic traits” mention, telling me I couldn’t diagnose another person. It almost defended the other person. I decided to argue that I was describing patterns of behavior, not making a diagnosis. Apparently, that was not enough to stop it from continuing on (and on and on) about it. The exchange felt a lot like one with someone who learns something and then regurgitates that information without any openness to nuance.

While it seemed to be trying to make me feel understood, it simultaneously invalidated me.

Through my experience, I noticed some potentially helpful uses for AI. I’m appreciating something I hadn’t expected: It supports my geeking-out tendencies. I love language and precision, and I’m learning to use AI to push me in those areas.

AI as a Tool for Critical Thinking and Communication

I know this might sound counterintuitive given some research findings, but in some ways, I think AI can help people practice their critical-thinking skills. (It does for me!) For example, AI may help in building communication skills. Yet because it can be quite literal and may not always detect sarcasm, double meanings, or passive-aggressive undertones, the suggestions AI provides can need adjustment to accurately express what people are trying to say.

When emotions are high and a response is needed quickly, the step of asking AI to take some of the emotional charge out of something or rephrase it in a kinder or more direct way, for example, can also offer a thoughtful interruption—a tool—potentially saving a person from a reactive interaction they may later regret.

All that said, AI's communication suggestions needed refining to truly meet my goals—especially the primary one of minimizing potential reactivity from the other party, which meant shoring up my own language.

My requests were simply communication prompts, which might be seen as "lower stakes"—not more complex requests for mental-health advice and support. Regarding higher-stakes advice, a BBC article summarized real-life experiences that struck me like an unexpected slap: “Designed to converse with users and create content requested by them, they [chatbots] have sometimes been advising young people on suicide, sharing health misinformation, and role-playing sexual acts with children.” Especially when someone is in a vulnerable space, yikes.

Tips for Potentially Healthier Use of AI

Remind yourself that it's not human. It can miss nuance, and it can respond in ways that seem designed to please you or agree with you. Just because something sounds validating doesn't necessarily mean it's accurate or helpful. Some AI is designed to keep you engaged.

Tell AI what you're trying to accomplish. Rather than sharing only your feelings and asking what to do, explain your goals. For example, “I want to express my frustration without escalating this conflict. Can you help me find a way to say this?” And then, check how it feels to you. Maybe test it on yourself or ask a friend how they'd react to being told the same thing.

Ask it to challenge you, not just agree with you. You might try, “What am I overlooking?” or “How might the other person interpret this?” You can also ask it to identify possible unintended consequences of its suggestions. Of course, asking these questions doesn't guarantee better advice, but it does help you explore.

Be careful about privacy. Before sharing personal information—names, email addresses, etc.—understand how that information might be stored or used. Consider whether identifying details about yourself or others are necessary for what you're asking.

Recognize when AI isn't an appropriate source of support. I wouldn't recommend using AI in place of human peer support, and it's not a substitute for clinical judgment, assessment, or treatment. People experiencing suicidality or other mental health crises need appropriate human support, including professional assessment and intervention when indicated.

Bottom Line

AI seems to be here to stay, so as a therapist, I’m bringing it up in sessions with transparency. For example, if clients say they checked with AI, I ask about their experience: What did the AI tell them? How did they feel about it? What worked for them about the answer, and what didn’t?

Just as it's beneficial to evaluate the information we're receiving online, we also need to evaluate what we're receiving from AI. Does it actually help us think more clearly, or is it just telling us what we want to hear?

For a few self-improvement or communication tools here and there, AI may be helpful. It also can offer advice that humans still need to sort through, evaluate, and adapt for themselves. Relying on it as a substitute for individualized mental health care may be downright dangerous.

item.title: Anxiety Is More Complex Than We Might Think
item.description:
Anxiety

Anxiety Is More Complex Than We Might Think

Underestimating anxiety's complexity can lead to disappointment in therapy.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic anxiety is a key symptom of complex trauma.
  • In therapy, over-simplification can lead to disappointment.
  • Recovery may require attention to many areas of life and a variety of approaches and may take time.
  • The therapist’s regulation of their own anxiety is key to the work.
Source: iStock by Getty Images

Anxiety can be a necessary response to potential threats, but also a serious chronic condition that negatively affects our functioning and well-being. In either case, we feel wary and on edge, scared or irritable, with overactive thoughts. We are tense and easily startled into more powerful fear responses.

The key factor is whether our fear-system, our biological responses to threat, can ‘switch off’ once the threat has passed. If we hear a strange creak alone in bed at night, we might tense up, hold our breath and listen carefully; our heart beating faster. If we hear it again and recognise the hot water pipe noises, we can relax and quickly fall back to sleep.

However, if anxiety is a habitual state, we might still guess that it was the hot water pipes, but we can’t relax—we keep imagining an intruder breaking in—staying awake for hours in a state of fear.

What is anxiety? The biological response is at the core, what I call fear-alert, our instinctive reaction to danger sensed at a distance.[1] Our hearing, eyesight, and sense of smell become more acute to evaluate the threat, and our startle response is readied, and the nerve signal regulating our heart rate is withdrawn. The ‘brake’ that holds our fear responses in check is removed. We are now ready for extreme life-saving action.

This means our nervous system is highly volatile now; even minor or imagined threats can put us in a high-energy state of fear-arousal—fight, flight, or freeze. In this state, the heart's pumping capacity shifts up a gear, and a flood of hormones enriches the bloodstream with glucose and other nutrients, providing sustained energy.

Because fear-alert frequently switches into fear-arousal, our experience of ‘anxiety’ covers fear-arousal symptoms, such as a racing heart, dry mouth, sweaty palms, nausea or numbness, as well as the wariness, irritability and worrying thoughts of fear-alert.

None of this would be a problem if our fear responses deactivated once the threat had passed. However, this can only happen when we feel safe. If we are under threat and don’t feel safe for long periods, the biological processes that switch off our fear responses start to lose effectiveness, and we can get stuck in fear-mode, a chronic state of fear-alert that frequently tips us into fear-arousal or fear-collapse [2] [3]. This is another way of talking about complex trauma, which affects many areas of life, as we can see in the following example:

Adrian was a young man with a responsible managerial job who suffered from constant high levels of anxiety and was unable to make decisions about work and relationships, leading to constant self-criticism. He worked for an aggressive boss who treated him like a slave.

He found all social interactions stressful and exhausting; he felt the need to please everyone and keep them entertained. This burden led him to avoid intimate relationships, and the relationships he had didn’t last long.

He experienced all his pain and confusion as being "in his head," with his mind always overactive but his body “numb from the neck down.”

I worked with Adrian for nearly five years. He had previously tried CBT and found it unhelpful. I felt under huge pressure to alleviate his anxiety quickly, which triggered my own fear responses, but our work was painfully slow.

It emerged that he had suffered from anxiety since he was 3 years old. He had been highly disturbed by his mother’s acute distress at the death of her own mother. This loss of his caregiver was compounded by a sense that he had caused her collapse, and throughout his childhood he constantly tried to make her happy, becoming overburdened by responsibility.

Understanding the impact of his early history interested Adrian; however, it did not alleviate his anxiety, and realising that he didn’t have to take responsibility for the happiness of others also changed nothing. Being stuck for many years in a continuous state of fear activation had created a complex tangle of problems: nervous system volatility, chronic bodily tension, the numbing of sensation, deeply ingrained patterns of thought and behaviour towards others, habitual self-criticism and an inability to seek care.

We explored all these areas with little success at first. What started to shift things, however, was understanding and regulating my own fear-system. I stopped reacting with anxiety to Adrian’s pressing need for a cure and stopped overworking. I became a calmer presence, and he responded, eventually able to engage with ways of working that were not initially helpful. We worked on regulating breathing and using a focus-oriented approach that gradually helped him become reconnected with his bodily sensations. [4]

By the time Adrian finished work, he had become far less of a people-pleaser, had changed his boss and asserted himself more at work. He was in a relationship where he was gradually allowing himself to accept care as well as give it, and his generalised anxiety had greatly diminished.

Anxiety can be highly complex, and treating it at the level of a thought disorder that needs correction can lead to disappointment and frustration. Treatment may take time, and it may consider many aspects and use several different approaches. It also requires the therapist to understand and regulate their own anxiety in the work.

item.title: Want More Out of Therapy? Let Your Therapist Know
item.description:
Therapy

Want More Out of Therapy? Let Your Therapist Know

No matter how great your therapist is, they can't read your mind.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists and clients both benefit if there is open, thoughtful communication about how therapy is going.
  • Giving honest feedback helps you, your therapist, and all of your therapist's future clients.
Source: Sasun Bughdaryan / Unsplash

"I like my therapist, but sometimes I wish they would just ask me more open-ended questions."

An amazing colleague, who is also professional coach, recently said this to me. This colleague shared how her therapist is brilliant and helpful, but often shifts too quickly into problem-solving mode. I inquired if my colleague had ever given her therapist this feedback and she shook her head. I asked her what stopped her and she replied that she just never thought of doing so, but felt that her therapist would likely respond positively if she did. I encouraged her, in the same way that I encourage you, dear reader, to regularly be sharing feedback in your sessions.

Feedback is key to a good working relationship

Licensed therapists have years of training, including learning about evidence-based practices and getting supervised training in providing therapy. Your therapist shows up to your sessions with a lot of knowledge and skill that can help you recognize patterns, process significant life events, and so much more. But no matter how amazing your therapist is, one thing that they can never know, unless you tell them, is how helpful (or not) you find their therapeutic approach and the information that they’re sharing with you.

Therapists try to build a strong rapport with you, as they know that having a strong therapeutic alliance is important for you to feel safe and fully engage in your session. Research tells us that the stronger a therapist’s interpersonal skills are, the more likely their patients are to return for another session.1 Nevertheless, the therapist cannot know if you do not understand the information that they are trying to share with you, or if it just doesn’t feel aligned with your perspective, unless you tell them. You, your therapist, and your work together will benefit from this information.

Questions for every session:

  1. What was helpful in session today?
  2. What could be even better yet?

Questions to ask periodically:

  1. What are your thoughts about the the work you are doing in therapy?
  2. What is going well overall?
  3. What could be even better yet?

You shouldn’t have to worry about your therapist’s reaction

It can feel awkward, giving feedback—especially if after reading this article, you’re the one who’s prompting such a discussion. (Feel free to share this article as a jumping off point for discussion in your therapy session!)

If part of the reason that you don’t want to give feedback to your therapist is because you are afraid that they will stop liking you, that is also really important information that you need to share with your therapist. There could be many reasons for you feeling this way, and they are all really important to identify and discuss in therapy.

It’s normal for you to want other people to like you. This is especially true of your therapist, with whom you have shared a lot of sensitive information about yourself. Therapists have an ethical obligation to do no harm, to try to benefit you with their care, to build trust, practice fairly and justly, and respect the dignity and privacy of all people. This means that the therapist needs to be making decisions based on what they feel is healthiest for you and the therapeutic relationship. Therefore, even if your feedback is somehow given in such a way that your therapist could feel negatively about it, that is not a reason that you would not share it.

Therapists cannot know how they can improve if they’re not getting feedback

A therapists job is to take in the information that you’re sharing and to consider how the therapy session could be augmented to better meet your needs. They will not stop liking you if you provide constructive feedback, and if you perceive that were somehow to be the case, that would be a really important area for discussion and ultimately may signal that you and your therapist are no longer a good fit.

The feedback you provide can help the therapist engage in shared decision-making with you to see if you need a new treatment approach, if they need to refer you to a colleague so you can meet with someone who specializes in a different areas (e.g., couples counseling or EMDR sessions). This could mean engaging with different clinicians for different treatments at the same time or pausing your current treatment while receiving this care.

For therapists

As a therapist, avoiding feedback doesn't mean you can assume a client is completely satisfied with the therapy: it more likely means you won't have a good understanding of the reasons why clients discontinue their sessions with you. Asking for feedback routinely normalizes the practice, helps you provide better care, and helps you learn and grow as a clinician so you can build your skills and continue benefiting your clients.

item.title: The Impact of a Psychopathic Mother
item.description:
Psychopathy

The Impact of a Psychopathic Mother

Lovelessness, guiltlessness, division, and confusion with a psychopathic mother.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Lovelessness and guiltlessness are fundamental traits of psychopathy.
  • Common signs of psychopathy are confusion and bad feeling.
  • Psychopaths often set one person against another, and though suspicion is rife, the cause is never rooted out.

When my children were young, I remember reading aloud children’s books that delighted both them and me. One book that especially comes to mind is Diane Goode’s Where’s Our Mama? 1 The author dedicated this book to her own mother, and her feelings for her mother are expressed through the two young children in the story. In the story, a gust of wind blew the mother’s hat off her head. When the mother went to fetch her hat, the two children became separated from her and began to cry. A policeman approached them as they searched for their mama and asked them to describe her. They quickly said she was the most beautiful and bravest person who always wears the prettiest hats, has a voice that everyone loves, and is the best cook in the world. Of course, they were all soon joyfully reunited.

As in the story, “mama” elicits an image of a loving, giving, selfless person. But some people never had such a mother. Many were born the children of psychopathic mothers. For those in such circumstances, what can they expect?

Source: kalhh / Pixabay

Insidious psychopathic abuse

According to psychopathy experts, Paul Babiak and Robert D. Hare, in their book, Snakes in Suits, “Psychopaths may push the envelope of acceptable human behavior … . Some psychopaths live in society and do not technically break the law—although they may come close, with behavior that usually is very unpleasant for those around them. Some may lead seemingly normal lives, not hurting people in ways that attract attention, but causing problems nonetheless in hidden economic, psychological, and emotionally abusive ways. They do not make warm and loving parents, children, or family members.”2

Lovelessness and guiltlessness

Having had a mother and sister who were highly psychopathic, I had eye-opening experiences from when I was young. I noticed early on that both my mother and sister were different from other mothers and other children that I knew. But it took years before I was able to understand the term that described their personality disorder. Their behavior displayed the psychopathic traits of lovelessness and guiltlessness, which sociologists William and Joan McCord have characterized as fundamental to the disorder.3

Realization provides explanation

In realizing this, I came to terms with the fact that my mother was the antithesis of the iconic mother. This realization has helped me to make sense of much of what I experienced and observed growing up. She consistently exhibited strange and unusual behavior. Previously, I could never understand why she hid and disregarded treasured family photographs. One day, I happened to find them hidden in a dark, clammy basement behind a piece of plywood on a cold, damp cement floor. They had not been placed there by accident. The age-old photographs were damaged by mildew and could not be replaced. When I asked her about it, she shrugged and was expressionless, showing her “I don’t care” attitude. She had no affection or regard for the warm memories the photos embodied. Instead, photographs of complete strangers were showcased in prominent places in the house for no apparent reason.

Division and confusion

My mother had many strategies to get her way by creating conflicts and division between family members and relatives. I witnessed these conflicts all my life at different times and in many situations. One day, I happened to call my mother, only to find out that my niece had recently been married. My mother’s voice could not have sounded more delighted to tell me that I was the only person not invited. She perpetuated ill will and division. According to psychologist Neville Symington, “One of the most evident signs of psychopathy is the presence of confusion and bad feeling. One person is set against another and suspicion is rife, but the cause is never rooted out.”4

The brush-offs and the slights were countless, and the cold treatment never changed, even during a time of great personal distress. In such a time, even a stranger can sympathize with someone going through hardship. Instead, my mother and sister went to an astrologer to find out if my life would be ruined and, on a telephone call, they blurted out in high-pitched laughter exactly what the future had in store for me. They tried to get me to believe I would be ruined. I didn’t believe, and it never occurred, but their diabolical scheming was another sign of their disorder.

In dreaming of what a mother is, I came to grips with the fact that I never had a mother like "mama," and that my mother could never be trusted.

item.title: Harms From Megan’s Law in America
item.description:
Sexual Abuse

Harms From Megan’s Law in America

Laws that were passed to protect us from molesters may actually do the opposite.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Child sexual exploitation is a real problem, but the perpetrators are rarely strangers.
  • Lifetime punishment for those who have already offended is not the best way to protect children.
  • Comprehensive school sex education helps children protect themselves from being molested.

Megan’s Law (1994), the Adam Walsh Act (2006), efforts to require special sex offender license plates, and dozens of other laws restrict the movement, residence, employment, privacy, and every other right of convicted sex offenders.

Megan’s Law was sponsored by New Jersey congressman Dick Zimmer, who recently died at age 81. Signed by then-President Clinton, the federal law required states and municipalities to set up websites listing the local addresses of convicted sex offenders who had completed their sentences.

The supposed reason for this is the familiar chant of every moral panic: “Helping families make informed decisions for themselves and their children.” Decisions about what? “Quick, change lanes, we don’t want to drive behind a molester.”

Predictably, these registries are used by vigilante groups attempting to drive registrants out of their community. Cities across America also require offenders to surrender their civil rights on Halloween—despite no evidence whatsoever of an uptick in offender activity. Laws regulate where registrants are allowed to live—requirements so stringent that they often end up under freeway overpasses, homeless camps, or in the desert. If they weren’t poor, sick, and hopeless before release, they are soon after.

Unfortunately, research shows that these laws do not make American children safer (1), and critics argue that they divert resources from more effective prevention.

  • Most sexual exploitation of children is done by a known person, not a stranger who can be avoided by studying a map. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention states that about 90 percent of child sexual abuse is perpetrated by someone known and trusted by the child or family. (2)
  • Registry populations are rarely the source of new child victimizations or repeated offenses. Most people convicted of sex offenses are not rearrested for another sex offense, and their overall rearrest rate is lower than that of other released prisoners. (3)
  • Demonizing registrants teaches kids the wrong self-protection strategies. “Stranger danger”—long promoted by disaster entrepreneurs like the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children—instills fear and undermines kids’ confidence and resilience.
  • Isolating registrants and making their lives impossible incentivizes them to acts of desperation, without the moderating effects of community. Rather than making everyone else safer, this makes them more dangerous.
  • The collateral consequences on the families of registrants include employment problems, housing disruption and homelessness, harassment, and stigma affecting registrants’ children. Undermining these innocent people’s ability to create a decent future weakens public safety.
  • Sex offender registration, notification, and segregation programs impose enormous costs on states and communities, and researchers question whether those costs buy any safety benefit. (4,5) None of the money spent on these programs can be available for alternative programs such as treatment and rehabilitation of offenders, supervision to mainstream them after release, and giving all children comprehensive school sex education (which has been shown to promote physical and mental well-being in a range of settings). (6)

Perhaps the worst thing about laws like these is that they reinforce the public’s terror and rage: terror about their ever-increasing sense of vulnerability; rage about their dreadful sense of powerlessness. Result: a bloodthirsty desire to punish someone, someplace, for destroying the pleasures of parenthood. Logic that would promote actual child safety is quickly overwhelmed by this raw emotion.

I’m quite sympathetic about how people are desperate to feel like they’re doing something to make themselves and their families safer. Given the constant reminders that the world is now too treacherous to let kids out of the house–courtesy of Fox “News,” Law & Order, Amber Alert, and the NRA–every reasonable American is scrambling to feel empowered. How can someone feel they’ve accomplished “I’m not gonna take it anymore”? Mess with the lives of hapless molesters.

There’s no data showing that any of these registration and segregation programs actually make our kids and communities safer. They certainly don’t make anyone feel safer—in fact, just the opposite. But they make people feel they’re doing something. These laws invariably pass without any research to show that they will benefit anyone besides the companies that administer these programs (creating and selling the special license plates, monitoring devices, etc.). Try a pilot program and evaluate after a year? Who has time for such thoughtfulness—we’re in a crisis!

Today, any public policy that helps people feel less powerless is perceived as good—even if it has no impact or makes a problem worse (for example, abstinence-only sex ed). And that makes frightening the public a smart political move for cynical people who want power.

item.title: Stop Playing the End of the Scene
item.description:
Career

Stop Playing the End of the Scene

To make the most of life's curveballs, you can take the next logical step.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Improv can offer a new model for thinking about dreams and goals.
  • Instead of focusing on the end goal, improv promotes just taking the next logical step.
  • A new book by Mary Lemmer highlights four improv principles that apply to everyday life.
  • 'Yes anding,' accepting situations, and making bold choices can keep you moving forward.
Source: Photo by Jon Tyson on Unsplash

While I was promoting my book, Play Your Way Sane, someone interviewing me said they admired my career trajectory. I had a goal in mind and worked toward it, single-mindedly.

I was taken aback. I may have even laughed because they couldn’t have been more wrong.

After college, I moved to New York City to become an actor. I hit the pavement, auditioned ruthlessly, and landed some film, TV, and theater jobs.

But then I hit my late twenties, and I definitely couldn't pay all my bills on my acting money. I went back to grad school to earn my Ph.D. and become a professor. But the professor jobs didn't pan out.

To pay the bills, I got a job as a teaching artist. One of my first placements was as the full-time English teacher in a public school in the Bronx, and I really enjoyed the work.

I went back to school again. I earned an MS.Ed. and teacher certification and became a full-time middle and high school teacher.

During that time, I had also been working on a book. Eventually, an editor at Simon & Schuster liked my manuscript, and they published my book, Play Your Way Sane. There was no master plan. The goals change and evolve. It’s a moving target. I get out of bed, put everything into whatever it is I’m pursuing, then wake up the next day and take the next logical step.

Source: Photo by Jukan Tateisi on Unsplash

How to Handle Anything

My career thus far only makes sense in retrospect and because I’ve approached jobs with the improvisational spirit of working with what’s in front of me and taking each logical next step. In Mary Lemmer’s new book, How to Handle Anything, she breaks down four improv concepts we can apply to live a better life—more in-the-moment, next-logical-step kind of life.

1. Say Yes, And

Instead of getting stuck on an end goal (in improv, pre-scripting the scene), saying Yes, And means you accept your situation as it develops and then roll with it.

This could mean:

  • Applying for different jobs when your current industry becomes oversaturated.
  • Going to couples counseling when your relationship is struggling.
  • Seeing a specialist when you get reports that your child is struggling at school.

It doesn’t mean liking your current reality. It means acknowledging your reality as it is, then figuring out how to take that next logical step.

2. Everything’s a Gift

Improvisers are conservationists; they use every morsel that’s handed to them to create unscripted scenes. In real life, this means making the most of what you get, instead of focusing on the opportunities you don’t have.

This could look like:

  • Accepting a less-than-ideal job offer and then making the most of it and working your way up the ladder.
  • Finding a better match when your previous boyfriend breaks up with you.
  • Putting your all into volunteer work and making lifelong friends there who help you network later.

3. Play the Scene You’re In

Playing the scene you’re in means accepting reality as it is, instead of complaining about it or living as if you’re in a different reality.

This could look like:

  • Telling people how you actually feel, instead of pretending to be happy.
  • Asking people for help when you’re struggling.
  • Focus on how you can help people and not just what you want to do.

4. Don’t Be Afraid to Get Weird

Improvisers aren’t afraid to make bold choices. Sometimes it pays off with a big laugh. Other times, it falls flat. But with big risks come big rewards, and at the very least, we learn from our mistakes.

This might mean:

  • Cold calling someone at the company you want to work for.
  • Putting your personality into your work, warts and all, instead of trying to do things like everyone else.
  • Combine your varied interests to carve out your own niche. Improv, psychology, and teaching anyone?

Stop Playing the End of the Scene: Take the Next Logical Step

Stop thinking about your life course as being linear. Life has twists, turns, and a tremendous amount of uncertainty. Improv helps us embrace and accept this uncertainty and focus on the here and now. We don’t have to know how the scene ends. We have to take one step, then another, then the next.

item.title: Supportive Design in the Waiting Room: Puzzles Anyone?
item.description:
Play

Supportive Design in the Waiting Room: Puzzles Anyone?

Puzzles may provide positive distraction, social support, and perceived control.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Little research has been done on the use of games and puzzles provided for adults in waiting rooms.
  • Puzzles can be worked on by multiple people, over time, and the work is not "owned" by any given individual.
  • Puzzles provide the opportunity to further understand the role of perceived control in healthcare.

On a recent trip to my dentist’s office for a dental cleaning appointment, I was pleasantly surprised to see a puzzle on the coffee table in the center of the waiting room. The puzzle was being worked on by a patient waiting for her appointment. There was already progress on this 500-piece Halloween-themed puzzle; the borders had been completed. When I came back to the office for a follow-up appointment a week later, there was even more progress. And this time, two waiting patients, sitting across from each other, were actively engaged with the puzzle.

Puzzles are a form of positive distraction in waiting rooms and elsewhere. Positive distraction is one of three pivotal variables in Ulrich’s theory of supportive design (Ulrich, 1991). The other two variables are social support and perceived control. Social support refers to the idea that elements in the surroundings, such as furnishings, can support visiting friends and relatives (the concept is usually applied to in-patient settings). Perceived control refers to the idea that the setting offers opportunities for the individual to make changes to the environment (i.e., for agency). An example would be turning lights on or off.

Positive Distraction

Positive distraction refers to the idea that there are pleasant elements in the surroundings that distract us from worrisome thoughts. Most often, positive distraction takes a visual form, such as a window view of nature or artwork, but positive distraction could also be provided by an auditory source, such as background music, which has been shown to lower anxiety in adults when played before a medical procedure (Biddiss et al., 2014). Closed-caption television is a somewhat trickier form of positive distraction to use, as the news on many channels may be upsetting rather than positively distracting. In the waiting room at my dentist’s office, there is a large wide-screen television hanging on the wall, but no news is played; rather, it plays old episodes of Antiques Roadshow, which seems fitting for New England, where I live.

Most often in the literature, games and puzzles (and coloring books) are associated with pediatric settings, but coloring has also been shown to decrease anxiety in parents waiting while their child is in surgery (Robinson et al., 2018). There is relatively little literature on the use of adult games and puzzles in healthcare settings. But not only do puzzles have the potential to offer positive distraction, but they also may engage perceived control. Of Ulrich’s three variables, it has been more difficult to show the impact of perceived control compared with the other elements. In research involving perceived control in outpatient waiting rooms (Devlin et al., 2023), the authors concluded that people likely have a schema that discourages manipulation of environmental elements, but that they are more likely to adjust controls when such controls are perceived to be individual (such as a table lamp next to your chair). In that study, a participant wrote, “I can’t rearrange items in the room without people wondering what I am doing,” which the authors argue suggests that “people have a script for the behaviors that are appropriate in a doctor’s waiting room.”

Puzzles and the Theory of Supportive Design

Puzzles offer the possibility of engaging all three of Ulrich’s variables. They offer the opportunity for positive distraction; they also accommodate social support because puzzles can be worked on by more than one person at a time. Further, there is perceived control because puzzles afford engagement (as demonstrated by the fact that the Halloween puzzle was being worked on in the dentist’s office—it invited participation). The notion of affordances comes from the work of American psychologist J. J. Gibson and refers to the idea that the environment offers opportunities that can readily be perceived. For example, a chair (as well as many other entities such as low tables and steps) affords sitting because we can see a horizontal platform to support us.

Puzzles as Research Opportunities

Given the schema mentioned earlier that people have a script guiding what behaviors are appropriate in the doctor’s waiting room, it isn’t clear what circumstances need to exist before people, of their own accord, would start working on a puzzle. For example, would people open a closed puzzle box and start working on it? Or would it take something like an open box, or an open box with a completed corner, for people to realize they were being “invited” to engage with the puzzle pieces?

Research investigating this puzzle process might help us better understand the role of the elements that invite (i.e., afford) perceived control in healthcare settings.

A Word About Contamination

Given concerns about contamination, research should also consider concerns that may be raised by handling items that others have handled. There may be different levels of acceptability to engaging with puzzles depending on the nature of the healthcare office. For example, would people be less concerned about engaging with a puzzle on a visit to the dentist for teeth cleaning than to a primary care provider during flu season?

item.title: Do Our Choices Reflect Our Values?
item.description:
Decision-Making

Do Our Choices Reflect Our Values?

How to close the gap between the values we hold and the choices we make.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Naming our values does not guarantee that our everyday choices will reflect them.
  • Repeated behaviors offer clues about our values, but we must consider the circumstances behind them.
  • Bringing values into focus can help us choose actions that speak to what we most care about.

We often hear about the importance of living according to our values. Yet asserting our values is not the same as examining how they shape our decisions. When we lose sight of them or face competing commitments and pressures, we can sometimes fail to act on them. On the other hand, understanding how to incorporate them into our decision-making can help us act on them more consistently.

What are values?

According to Lilach Sagiv and colleagues, personal values are “broad desirable goals that motivate people’s action and serve as guiding principles in their lives.”

As goals, values are not directed towards specific achievements but rather guide decisions across various aspects of our lives. For example, people who value honesty will try to tell the truth and seek out honest people wherever they may be, whether at work, at home, or elsewhere.

Values are desirable, and we think they are worth pursuing, and we want to pursue them consistently, even when other desires compete with them. However, competing desires may capture our attention. For example, ordering a second dessert at a celebratory meal does not necessarily mean I no longer value my long-term health. In this particular instance, I may simply be making an exception to how I usually act on that commitment.

As guiding principles, values serve not only as the lens through which we perceive our experiences, but they also become strong factors in how we choose to act. For example, people who value autonomy over security may see their job as stifling and look for other opportunities; those who value security over autonomy see the same job as stable and dependable.

When I talk about values, I like to say that values are things that we value, things we care about. This simple sentence shifts our attention from abstract concepts to the things we hold close and see as part of who we are. It also lets us see the difference between ordering that second dessert and working to be trustworthy. The former satisfies a momentary desire; the latter speaks to an enduring concern.

Do actions speak louder than words?

Comparing what we say matters to us with how we consistently act can reveal a gap between our values and behavior. Imagine someone who says they value their personal relationships, but they repeatedly choose work over spending time with friends and family. This discrepancy between what a person says and what they do should bring reflection. It may be that the person does value personal relationships, but their competing value of financial security or personal ambition has a stronger influence on their decision-making. Alternatively, they may truly prioritize personal relationships but lose sight of values when responding to workplace demands. Sometimes, however, someone may recognize their priorities clearly and still have limited freedom to act because their job is insecure or their family depends on their income. Importantly, we can examine whether our repeated behaviors reflect what we value and consider what choices would help us act more consistently on what we care about.

Bringing values into our lives

Bas Verplanken and Rob Holland found that values influence people’s choices and behavior when they are brought into focus and when those values are central to the person’s self-concept.

To bring your values into your choices and actions, follow these four steps:

  1. Identify what matters to you in each situation: Ask yourself, “What do I care about with respect to this situation, and how do I want to respond?” Consider both the outcome you hope for and the values you want your actions to express.
  2. Examine competing concerns and pressures: Ask, “Is anything pulling me in different directions?” In certain situations, you may see competing values, people’s expectations, or practical constraints. Consider which concerns deserve priority, which constraints you must work within, and which expectations you could question.
  3. Choose an action that aligns with your values and priorities: Ask, “What options would allow me to act on what matters most to me while still attending to my other concerns?” Identify specific actions you can take, anticipate what might make acting difficult, and consider how you can remove or lessen any obstacles (both internal and external).
  4. Reflect on what happened: Ask, “How well did my response express my values, and what could I change next time?”

With regular practice, your values will become more than a list of admirable qualities; they will shape your goals, guide your decisions, and motivate you to act on what matters to you.

item.title: Helping Your Child Navigate Emotions When You're Overwhelmed
item.description:
Parenting

Helping Your Child Navigate Emotions When You're Overwhelmed

A two-for-one approach to go from spiraling to options—for you and your child.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • It's normal for parents to feel overwhelmed when their child is upset. We can't fix their problems for them.
  • Build lasting skills by processing with them, not for them. Start with empathy and honoring their distress.
  • Pinpoint the thoughts under the feeling, fact check interpretations, and generate new perspectives.
Parents can feel stressed when their kids are stressed out.
Source: Anastasiia Havrysh / iStock

We’ve all been there. Your 4-year-old can only find one of their spaceman boots and is in total meltdown; your middle schooler begs not to go to school because they’re convinced they have no one to sit with at lunch; your teen has stormed off when you simply asked if they started their homework. Meanwhile, you are just trying to make it through the finish line of the day. Somehow, it’s not looking good.

Our overwhelm meets their distress. It’s a stressful emotional gridlock.

Forward Is Toward: Carry Your Child’s Emotions With Them, not for Them

Our overwhelm often comes from feeling like we have to change course: Do an abrupt swerve to stop or fix what our kids are feeling. And of course, it’s not like our kids don’t want that, but it’s not like that’s all they want either. Witness how, when we make a beeline for solutions, kids often respond with: “You don’t understand! You’re just trying to fix it! You never listen to me!”

But rather than whisking them away from their feelings, our best move is to go toward their emotions with them.

What is the best way for kids to process their emotions? I have created a process I call the Seven Shifts, and it works for any age—parents and kids alike.

Getting Our Bearings First: Try the Route Yourself

The Seven Shifts is a repeatable throughline for any emotional situation; it involves first honoring what you’re feeling so you can settle back into a more thoughtful (versus reactive) state, then toggling to what the feeling is pointing to: the need for us to do our good work—zoom in and understand what our thoughts are telling us, then zoom out to question interpretations and consider other possibilities that are more helpful and… true.

It looks like this:

Shift 1: Empathize—don’t fight or fix the feeling; just make room for it

Notice how just saying to yourself: “I’m worried for my child, or even I’m frustrated and too tired, and that’s OK” allows your body to soften. You’re not fighting where you are. You aren’t saying you don’t care; your caring is not up for debate. You are validating your own experience—it’s a place where people land. Lots of people.

Same for your child: Instead of rushing to reassure or correct—get to what I call the “nodding head of agreement.” Your child sees that you see where they are: “This is really upsetting you. This is a lot you’re carrying. You really didn’t want it to be like this.” It’s not about agreeing with the logic; it’s accepting without judgment—this is where your child has landed.

Shift 2: Name it—what am I feeling?

Often in a blur of competing feelings, we feel lost—and when we feel lost, we spiral. The antidote? Just start naming the feelings—there may be several, and they may seem like opposites—like loving and frustrated. They are what I call “Emotion Neighbors”—opposites can sit side by side and not add up: feeling frustrated and sad, hopeful and exhausted.

Kids may not be able to name their feelings—ask: Does it feel mad, like something isn’t OK with you, or more hurt, like something is missing?

Shift 3: Settle inside—slow down and reset

The body registers all the stress of our thoughts. Tiny resets, a big exhale, a sigh, help you shift out of crisis mode and into connection. Bringing your calm to your child helps them find their calm, too. Sometimes it’s invisible—just your slow breathing helps them find their calm. A regulated nervous system is the foundation of everything that follows.

Shift 4: Zoom in and find “the gems”

What are the thoughts underneath the feelings? When we can find those gems—not necessarily positive—they tell us what we’ve been telling ourselves; knowing the narrative we’re reading helps point to what we need to reinterpret. When thoughts operate freely under our awareness, we get stuck in spirals of fear, frustration, or helplessness. Ask your child: “What’s your brain telling you? What is the alarm, going beep-beep-beep, in your mind?”

Shift 5: Zoom out—prism it to see multiple perspectives

Now that we’ve unearthed those gems, hold them up to the light and get different perspectives—translation: the things we say to ourselves unchecked we’d never say to a friend in a similar situation. We can fact-check our beliefs and edit accordingly and encourage our kids to do the same.

Help kids get in the habit of what I call “second-opinion thinking”: What would they tell a friend in that situation? What would a friend tell them? What would a hero or mentor say? Notice you’re not saying: “You’re thinking the wrong thing.” It’s an invitation: “Those thoughts sound like what anxiety says; can we fact-check it and see what else is more true?”

Shift 6: Take action one small step at a time

Equipped with a newer, truer story, is there a step you want to take that could help—like allowing yourself a “time out” and coming back to your child when you’ve had a second to reset? Or reminding yourself of your child’s strengths rather than just focusing on what’s wrong?

With your child, ask: “What’s a step that you could try—approaching a fearful situation? Saying something assertive to a friend? Scheduling grief time every day?”

Shift 7: Take stock and give credit where it is due!

We are the heroes of our lives, and our successes are in the tiny moments—notice them, and give credit where credit is due. Help them notice the progress they are making—and the way they made it—especially when things are hard. That’s how they will know how to value the steps along the way, not just the great moments across the finish line.

When we allow ourselves to turn toward—not away—from our emotions, the seven shifts become a two-for-one route toward understanding. Kids gradually learn the way from our responses and increasingly trust that they’ll come out with a better understanding of themselves and the world on the other side of the journey.

Here’s to better emotional navigation all around.

item.title: Helping Your Child Get Started With Schoolwork
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

Helping Your Child Get Started With Schoolwork

Practical strategies for parents to help kids manage schoolwork.

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Help your child build better homework habits by teaching them how to plan, manage time, and get started.
  • Simple strategies can make homework less stressful.
  • The goal is to help children become more independent, responsible, and confident in managing their schoolwork.

How many times have you heard or asked:

"Did you finish your homework?"

"I'll do it later."

"Did you study for your test?"

"I'm going to."

"Have you checked your assignments?"

"Yes, it’s fine"

Then you check your child’s grade portal and realize that homework and assignments are missing, or test grades look like there was never any real studying done. Does this pattern sound familiar?

For many families, getting homework completed or preparing for a test or quiz is not just an academic challenge but, rather, a daily struggle involving motivation, time management, initiation or getting started, planning, and follow-through. Parents become frustrated because their children seem capable of doing the work but struggle to get started. Children become frustrated because they feel nagged, overwhelmed, or misunderstood.

When executive functioning skills are still developing, telling a child to "just get it done" isn’t addressing the struggles. Instead, we need to help children learn how to get started, manage their time, work through resistance, and follow a plan, even when they would rather be doing something else.

Here are a few strategies to try with your child or teen:

Find the Sweet Spot of Time to Do the Hard Work

Not every child is ready to tackle demanding work the moment they walk through the door after school. Many children and teens have spent the entire school day working hard to manage their attention, behavior, emotions, and social interactions. By the time they get home, they are mentally exhausted.

Rather than expecting your child, who has spent a ton of mental, physical, and emotional energy all day, to be able to jump right into their homework assignments, build in a break for your child or teen so he or she can decompress for one hour. A snack, movement, music, time outdoors, or a little quiet time may help them transition from school to home. Set a timer and, after one hour, take out school materials with your child or teen in one consistent space in your home, and review the assignments that need to be completed.

What you are doing is building in a time to disconnect from school, then reconnect in a calm way and tackle the assignments that need to be completed. The goal is to find the sweet spot when your child is most ready to engage in undesirable tasks that require attention and follow-through to get them done.

Turn Planning Into a Game

Executive functioning practice does not have to feel like another lecture. Our children can be more engaged when they can participate in a challenge, solve a problem, or compete against their own performance. On a separate pad of paper or a large or small whiteboard, have your child write down the assignments that need to be completed for the night. Then, ask your child or teen to predict how long an assignment will take to complete and write it down. For example, you can ask your child or teen, "How long do you think these 12 math problems will take?" Set the timer and let your child go. When the timer rings, your child can then see how accurate he or she was about the duration of the assignment. If she finishes before the timer, awesome! If he needs more time, estimate how much longer based on how many problems were completed during the time frame. Set the timer again and go! Over time, your child or teen will be able to form a more realistic sense of how long an assignment will take to complete.

This process accomplishes yet another goal, and that is that it goes against the innately held idea that “My homework is gonna take forever!” This puts a time limit on homework assignments so that there is an end time. The goal is to finish the assignments rather than sitting at a desk or table for hours at a time with very little work actually completed.

Then number the assignments in the order to be completed. For example, will he want to start on the hardest assignment first? Will she want to start on the assignment that takes the shortest amount of time? Having a choice also helps initiation.

You can also turn planning into a challenge by encouraging your child or teen to get the work done so they can have downtime for the rest of the evening. Kids and teens alike are often surprised when a parent or executive functioning coach emphasizes the importance of downtime and the need for it. Ultimately, the focus is not on speed or perfection but, rather, on developing awareness, planning, and problem-solving.

Ask Questions Instead of Giving Orders

When children struggle with executive functioning, parents often become the source of every answer. In all transparency, many parents don’t want this role. They don’t want to be aware of and on top of every aspect of their child’s life to create movement. How many times have you heard yourself, as a parent, say things like:

  • Do your math first.
  • Study for science tonight.
  • Put your phone down.
  • Start your essay now.

Although these directions may be reasonable, your child or teen is not learning how to come up with their own strategies, and then they are dependent on you to get homework and other daily tasks done. If you happen to forget to verbalize the instruction or order, then it doesn’t get done. That is also maddening for a parent and creates an environment that supports your child or teen’s responses of “I don’t know. You didn’t tell me.”

Instead, ask questions that encourage accountability and a sense of responsibility:

  • What needs to get done tonight?
  • Which assignment is hardest to start?"
  • "What could make it easier?"
  • "What would you suggest if a friend were struggling with this?"
  • "What might your teacher recommend?"

You can guide your child or teen without making every decision for them. If the plan is unrealistic, help your child evaluate it. If she becomes stuck, offer a hint or a choice. But whenever possible, allow him to do the thinking. The more opportunities children have to formulate ideas, test strategies, and reflect on the results, the more practice they have to use their executive functioning skills.

Remember this: You are building skills for life. Executive functioning development takes time, and our kids and teens need opportunities to practice planning, managing time, initiating tasks, and following through. We can provide structure, encouragement, and accountability, but we also need to leave room for them to think, try, make mistakes, and learn from experience.

item.title: Happy Hybrid Helix 2026: Uncomfortable Truth at 4 Years of ChatGPT
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Happy Hybrid Helix 2026: Uncomfortable Truth at 4 Years of ChatGPT

What happens when AI strengthens while our natural intelligence is under increasing strain?

Posted November 10, 2026

Key points
  • Human intelligence includes curiosity, compassion, reasoning, imagination, and moral judgment.
  • Technological efficiency cannot guarantee environmental sustainability when overall demand keeps expanding.
  • The danger lies in assuming that strengthening AI automatically strengthens the world in which it operates.
Natural intelligence and artificial intelligence are increasingly interwoven, mutually influencing each other and our experience of "reality."
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

On November 30, 2022, ChatGPT entered public life. Four years later, artificial intelligence (AI) can write, code, translate, analyze medical images, and solve problems that once required years of specialist training. The progress is extraordinary. Yet the anniversary raises an uncomfortable question: What happens when the intelligence we manufacture grows stronger while the natural intelligence (NI) on which our lives depend comes under increasing strain? Welcome to the "Hybrid Helix"!

Imagine two intertwined strands. One represents NI, encompassing human minds and the living systems of our planet. The other represents AI, the technological capabilities we have created. Both influence each other. Both shape our future. Since 2022, however, their trajectories have become increasingly unequal. Our machines are gaining capabilities at remarkable speed. Meanwhile, our willingness to exercise independent judgment faces new pressures, and the natural systems sustaining human civilization continue to deteriorate.

The Hybrid Helix captures this growing imbalance. We are getting increasingly capable of doing things while becoming ever less able to decide what is worth doing and to perform what matters without crutches.

Four years that changed the balance

The numbers tell an extraordinary story. In 2022, conversational AI was still unreliable at many demanding intellectual tasks. By 2025, leading systems were meeting or exceeding human reference scores on several advanced scientific and mathematical benchmarks. Their ability to operate computers also advanced rapidly, with success on a demanding computer-use benchmark rising from approximately 5 percent in 2024 to 66 percent in 2025. (AI remains inconsistent and unreliable, but the trend of growing improvement is clear.)

Adoption has followed. According to the Stanford AI Index 2026, generative AI reached an estimated 53 percent of population adoption in the countries measured, and organizational AI adoption reached 88 percent at the time of writing. Today, more than four in five American high-school and college students use AI for school-related tasks. What began as an optional experiment is becoming part of everyday infrastructure. These advances offer genuine benefits. Humans with limited resources can access expertise, overcome language barriers and accomplish work that previously seemed beyond reach. The question is whether our human and environmental foundations are developing with comparable strength.

The first weakening strand: our minds

Human intelligence involves far more than producing correct answers. It includes curiosity, compassion, reasoning, imagination, and moral judgment. These capacities develop through experience and effort. Both are arenas that are shrinking as we are delegating more and questioning less. An eight-week experiment published in August 2026 followed 168 university students completing academic writing tasks. Those using AI freely achieved strong results with assistance. When subsequently tested without AI, students whose AI use had been restricted and combined with reflection performed better on measures of independent writing, reasoning and revision. The study has methodological limitations, but it illustrates a crucial distinction: A better finished product does not necessarily mean a more capable person.

A 2026 review of 89 studies found that AI's cognitive effects depend heavily on how it is used. Structured assistance can strengthen learning, while unrestricted reliance raises concerns about analytical autonomy and cognitive offloading. We cannot conclude that humanity has become less intelligent over these four years. There is no reliable global measure supporting that claim. What we can observe is the rapid expansion of opportunities to outsource thinking, alongside evidence that certain forms of dependence can undermine independent performance. We are hoarding AI while neglecting the conditions from which natural intelligence arises.

The second weakening strand: planet Earth

Here the deterioration is measurable across decades, including the four years since ChatGPT's launch. In 2022, five of the nine recognized planetary boundaries had been assessed as exceeded. By 2023, improved assessments identified six. In 2025, ocean acidification became the seventh. The September 2026 Planetary Health Check confirms that seven of nine boundaries are now breached, with pressure increasing across all seven. The changing count partly reflects advances in measurement, while the underlying deterioration is well established.

The irony is difficult to ignore. AI requires substantial physical infrastructure, including electricity, water, minerals, and land. In 2022, data centers, AI and cryptocurrencies together consumed approximately 460 terawatt-hours of electricity worldwide. By 2025, data-center electricity demand alone was growing by 17 percent annually, with AI-focused facilities expanding faster still. The April 2026 energy assessment projects that data-center electricity consumption could double by 2030. AI can also improve energy efficiency, scientific discovery, and environmental monitoring. These benefits require deliberate investment. Yet technological efficiency cannot guarantee environmental sustainability when overall demand keeps expanding. Let's face it—we are building increasingly powerful artificial systems on a natural foundation whose resilience is already compromised.

When the strands pull apart

The Hybrid Helix presents a challenge that technological progress alone will not resolve. As AI grows more capable, we may increasingly depend on it to address problems created by our own behavior, including excessive consumption, poor judgment, and environmental degradation. Greater artificial capability can even accelerate these pressures when efficiency encourages more production, consumption, and dependence. Inevitable collapse is not written into this trajectory. Our minds are (still) capable of learning and adapting. Our ecosystems can (still) recover when pressure is reduced. AI can contribute to both. The danger lies in assuming that strengthening AI automatically strengthens the world in which it operates.

Four years after ChatGPT's arrival, we must have a hard look at our definition of "progress": Are we becoming better at living well, or merely better equipped to produce more?

Triple H-HELP: Three actions for your hybrid future

  1. HEAR: Go beyond the familiar arguments about AI. Listen to people who benefit from it, those who struggle with it, and those whose voices rarely enter the debate. Ask whose interests are represented, who bears the costs, and what remains unexamined. Make a habit of seeking one credible perspective that challenges your own.
  2. HARMONIZE: Decide what you want from your hybrid future and align your daily behavior accordingly. If you value independent thinking, write your first argument before consulting AI. If you want to strengthen your memory, practice recalling information before searching for it. If environmental responsibility matters, examine your consumption, including digital consumption. Make sure your tools serve your ambitions.
  3. HEAL: AI will not save us from ourselves. Identify something in your life that needs attention and address it in the real world. Repair a relationship, improve a habit, spend time outdoors, participate in your community, or seek help with a problem you have been avoiding. Technology can support these efforts. The responsibility to act remains ours.

item.title: A Banned Author’s Fight Against Censorship
item.description:
Stress

A Banned Author’s Fight Against Censorship

Author George M. Johnson on book banning, mental health, and how books save lives.

Posted November 10, 2026

While censorship can harm the mental health of students, librarians, and authors, diverse bookshelves can heal, offering solidarity, community, and hope between the pages.

Emmy-nominated, award-winning, and bestselling Black nonbinary author and activist George M. Johnson wrote one of the most banned books in recent history and experienced the detrimental mental health impacts that followed, from the devastation of hatred to the realities of fearing for their life.

Still, Johnson courageously continues to write books that save lives, and fights to keep books on the shelves of libraries and schools that offer a mirror for every young person to find themselves in.

Author and activist George M. Johnson wrote one of the most banned books in recent history, and experienced the detrimental mental health impacts that followed. Their latest memoir, And If I Die Before I Wake, is now available.
Source: Vincent Marc/Used with permission

Q: Tell us about your journey as author of the previous #1 most banned book in America, All Boys Aren’t Blue, a memoir for teens about growing up Black and queer. What was it like for you to courageously share your story, only to have the book banned?

George M. Johnson: I remember the day I got the call that an offer was made for All Boys Aren't Blue. I was a freelance journalist and working part-time doing accounting, doing everything to make ends meet, and it was one of the best days of my life. Then an "Oh Sh**" moment hit me when I realized that I was going to have to be so vulnerable and so transparent with the world, and that's scary to know that your story will be out there for the masses to pick apart. But I couldn't have been more wrong. From the moment it released, I was getting texts and dm's and seeing so many comments about how the book was helping so many, and how so many were being seen and how for some, the book saved their life.

When the bans started, I thought it would just be a blip on the radar. But then I realized it was a fight that was choosing me and I decided to get very active. I went to school board meetings, and started writing about the bans and became one of the faces of fighting against censorship. I knew I had a duty to every young adult who didn't feel seen or heard, like I felt as a teenager.

I could've never imagined that the book would become one of the most banned books in the last 35 years and the most banned and challenged book in 2024. I sat in my apartment when I got the news that it hit #1 on the banned book list. It was hard to digest. It was hard to sit with how much hatred was in the world simply because I chose to tell my truth. I remember unplugging from social media for a few weeks to really gather my thoughts on how I felt and how I wanted to move forward. I realized that the goal was for me to become silent. So that even when I was hurt or harmed by the attacks on my work, it was still my duty to continue to write and speak out.

Q: As one of the leading voices fighting book bans and censorship, what are your thoughts on the mental health impacts of book banning?

George M. Johnson: The mental health impacts are immeasurable, in my opinion. When one writes a book, they know there may be some pushback a bad review or people who don't like it. When one writes a book that gets banned, it comes with other dangers that most authors could never imagine. The number of death threats I've had is countless. Being approached in an airport by someone who was a book-banning parent who recognized me, and got so loud that I was going to have to fight him. I don't think people realize the danger of being a creative and an artist is only heightened when you become banned.

So safety is a constant thought on my mind. That can easily lead to being more reclusive. It also makes authors not want to write certain books or subjects, which only hurts the readers who need it. As a writer, we are often isolated as we don't have co-workers and are often alone when writing. So it's stressful when dealing with it alone. And that stress can easily lead to a place where it becomes hard to write or hard to create. But I still find a way to break through that every time because I know the importance of storytelling and books save lives.

Q: Why is it important for all children and teens to find stories on the shelf at school and the local library that reflect their own identities and family structures?

George M. Johnson: Can you imagine waking up every day and looking in the mirror and not seeing your own reflection? That’s what it feels like when you can't pull a book off the shelf that speaks to you and your story and how you can navigate life. Books offer hope and optimism when things are going tough. Books provide fun and excitement on rainy days.

Even more, being seen in a story can fight the loneliness one may feel when they don't feel represented in their classrooms or in their communities. I remember being 15 and feeling alone and pretty isolated. I wish I had some of the books I've written back then so that I knew that I existed somewhere else in the world and that there were people and characters out there like me. Characters that helped me to understand that there were better days ahead and that there was light at the end of the tunnel.

Q: How can readers advocate for diverse bookshelves in their local schools and libraries?

George M. Johnson: We have to be active within our local politics. It all starts there. Going to the school board meetings and requesting certain books to be on the shelf. Making your voice be heard is super important. Also starting book clubs and doing free libraries when the books aren't on the shelf. Sometimes we have to pick up the gap where funding is missing for these life-saving books to be on the shelves.

Q: As your first adult memoir, And If I Die Before I Wake, is released, what do you hope readers take away from spending time with your story?

George M. Johnson: I really hope that this book helps people to understand the many different versions of self we will go through in life. Like I've had versions of myself die many times and you bury those past versions of self. I think this book helped me to go revisit those graves. Show those old versions of self how necessary it was for me to have to go through what I went through to get to this point today.

This book is about self-reflection and realizing the power that comes when we heal ourselves. Our lives are the sum of all the good and the bad, and the ups and the downs. It's important that we reflect on those things from time to time to help us heal and grow.
